summary: The `post_topics` field doc states the patterns are "NEVER subscribed / caught up on / announced in presence - that stays the explicit `topics` list". They ARE announced in presence: transport/presence-loop.ts:78 reads `allow.patterns()` and puts the raw regex sources into every beat's `postTopics` field, declared at engine/presence-beat.ts:85. This doc block ships verbatim in dist/config.d.ts (index.test.ts's own shippedBlocks reasoning notes ConfigObject's private field docs land in ConfigSchema's shipped type), so it is the specification an operator and an out-of-tree embedder read.
failure: Operator writes `post_topics: ["ctx-acquisition-project-nimbus-.*"]` after reading the doc's assurance that these are never announced in presence. On the first heartbeat the bridge posts the literal string `ctx-acquisition-project-nimbus-.*` to the shared `parley-presence` topic, readable by every other participant on that backend. The repo's own suite demonstrates this at config.test.ts:797 (WIRE_VALUES entry `{ beatField: 'postTopics', configPath: ['post_topics'] }`).
remediation: Rewrite the sentence to separate the two claims that are currently fused: patterns are never subscribed to and never enter catch-up (true), but ARE advertised on the presence topic as `postTopics` so peers can compute hand-off reachability (engine/presence-reach.ts) - and therefore must not encode anything an operator considers confidential. Mirror the same sentence in packages/bridge-core/README.md's `post_topics` line, which today says only "(not subscribed)" and is silent about the broadcast.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "a config field's own doc contradicts what the wire carries", not this sentence. config.test.ts already derives WIRE_VALUES = the set of config paths that reach a presence beat, and already proves that derivation complete ('covers every beat field fed from the config'). Add a case that, for each WIRE_VALUES row, reads the JSDoc block immediately above that field in config.ts (using the brace-walking scanner index.test.ts already implements in `scan`) and fails if it matches /never|not .*(announced|advertised|broadcast|published)/i. That fires for any future field whose doc claims locality while the beat carries it.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: Nothing executable - it is a comment edit. The only code I depend on being unchanged is transport/presence-loop.ts:78 `const postTopics = allow.patterns();` and its use at line 93, the branch that makes the current text false.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found - I grepped for the claim string across the repo (only config.ts:86 carries it) and no test asserts on comment text. source-hygiene.test.ts lints bridge-core comments for backend package names, tracker ids and self-dating phrases; a replacement avoiding those three shapes passes. I did not run the suite with the edited comment applied.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes only the false statement. If the real defect is judged to be the broadcast itself - an operator's regex sources naming internal projects going to a shared topic every peer reads - then correcting the doc leaves that disclosure fully in place and merely documents it. That is a separate adjudication about presence-loop.ts, which this target does not own.

The suite calls itself 'every documented capacity is pinned to a value, not only to itself', but only capacities exported from those four files are ever discovered. CLAUDE.md's standing rule for architectural tests is explicit: "Prefer, always: a glob over `src/**` rather than one file path."
failure: I appended `export const MAX_UNGRADED_THING = 7;` to allowlist.ts and `export const MAX_ANOTHER_THING = 9;` to mentions.ts. `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core/src/stated-bounds.test.ts packages/bridge-core/src/index.test.ts` -> 97 passed, 0 failed. Both are exactly the `^export const (MAX|MIN|DEFAULT)_...` shape the scan looks for; they are simply in files the list does not name. The same hole covers the five capacities already exported from engine/presence-beat.ts (MAX_RECORD_TOPICS, MAX_INSTANCE_ID_LEN, MAX_HANDLE_LEN, MAX_TOPIC_LEN, MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_MS), none of which is pinned to a literal anywhere.
remediation: Replace CAPACITY_MODULES with a recursive walk of src/**/*.ts minus *.test.ts (source-hygiene.test.ts already has `sourceFiles`, index.test.ts already has `sources`, so reuse one). Note honestly that this makes the guard RED until a CAPACITIES row exists for every constant it then discovers.

Make the discovery a glob and add a self-check row: the case that pins the discovered set must also assert the walk found at least one constant in a SUBDIRECTORY, not just src/ root, so a future refactor that collapses the walk back to a flat listing reddens. That grades the invariant (every exported capacity is pinned) from a place a move cannot invalidate.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: The regex `^export const ((?:MAX|MIN|DEFAULT)_[A-Z0-9_]+)\b` already in the test, plus a directory walk equivalent to source-hygiene.test.ts's `sourceFiles`.

A src/** glob discovers roughly a dozen additional constants across engine/, transport/ and auth/, and `expect(declared.sort()).toEqual(CAPACITIES.map(c => c.name).sort())` goes red until a row is written for each. That is real work, not a one-line change: each row needs an `expected` literal and a realistic-input probe.

I confirmed the extra constants exist by grepping engine/presence-beat.ts; I did not apply the glob and run it.

summary: `MIN_HASH_LEN = 10` is 10 hex digits = 40 bits, and it is exported from the public barrel (index.ts:10). Twelve lines below it, DEFAULT_HASH_LEN's doc argues at length that 40 bits is not enough: "That is why 40 bits was not enough: over the Matrix alias fold ... three lossy positions in a victim topic already put a collision in reach, and a collision routes one topic's traffic into another's backend channel." safeName accepts `hashLen: 10` and mints exactly that suffix.
failure: `safeName(asTopic(t), matrixAliasFold, { hashLen: MIN_HASH_LEN })` returns `<sanitized>-<10 hex>`. An out-of-tree plugin author reading the barrel sees a constant documented as "Shortest disambiguating suffix safeName will mint" and picks it as the sanctioned floor; they get the width the sibling doc says is brute-forceable over the very fold it names. stated-bounds.test.ts:76 actively pins this acceptance ('safeName hash suffix floor (MIN_HASH_LEN) accepts the bound itself'), and topic-name.test.ts:295 compounds it with a comment that is now wrong - "A 10-hex tail is no longer a shape safeName can mint" - true only for the default options, not for a legal call.
remediation: Raise MIN_HASH_LEN to DEFAULT_HASH_LEN (16) so the legal range is [16, 40] and there is no width the module documents as insufficient. If a narrower suffix must stay reachable for a backend with a hard name-length limit, keep it but state the exposure in MIN_HASH_LEN's own doc rather than in DEFAULT_HASH_LEN's - a reader picking the floor never reads the default's doc.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "a range check admits a value another doc in the same module argues is unsafe", not the number. In stated-bounds.test.ts, assert the accepted range's floor equals the security parameter the module actually mints by default (MIN_HASH_LEN >= DEFAULT_HASH_LEN), so any future re-widening has to change that relationship deliberately. Pair it with a table over the shipped folds measuring, for each, how many raw topics share a sanitized form - the search space the doc's argument turns on - so the constant is justified by a computation rather than by prose.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `if (!Number.isInteger(hashLen) || hashLen < MIN_HASH_LEN || hashLen > MAX_HASH_LEN) throw new RangeError(...)` at topic-name.ts:66 - the only place the floor is enforced, and the error message interpolates MIN_HASH_LEN so it stays coherent after the change.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: safeName(t, fold, { hashLen: 10 }) through { hashLen: 15 }. No shipped backend passes hashLen at all (every one omits it and gets DEFAULT_HASH_LEN), so no channel name in any existing deployment changes - this is not a rename event.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: stated-bounds.test.ts CAPACITIES row `{ name: 'MIN_HASH_LEN', actual: MIN_HASH_LEN, expected: 10 }` fails on 'pins MIN_HASH_LEN to a literal'; that row must be updated to 16, which is exactly the deliberate-change gate it exists to be. topic-name.test.ts:140 `it.each([MIN_HASH_LEN, MIN_HASH_LEN + 1, 20, MAX_HASH_LEN])` and :133's rejection list ([0,1,2,4,8,...]) are derived or below the new floor, so they still pass. stated-bounds' inside/outside probes are derived from b.bound and follow. I traced these by reading; I did not apply the change and run.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes the exported-floor hazard. It changes nothing a deployment runs on today (nothing mints below 16), so if the concern is an existing deployment already using a narrow suffix, raising the floor does not migrate it - it only stops the next caller. It also leaves the stale comment at topic-name.test.ts:295 wrong in the other direction.

summary: The file header states its own contract: "The screen's only real contract: whatever it accepts must MATCH in bounded time, for every input a caller can reach it with." The timing case is `it.each(CORPUS...)` - 35 hand-written sources plus family variants. ALL_CANDIDATES, which adds 40k+ generated sources (enumerateSources(3), quantifierShapes(), sampleSources(30_000, 4, 8)), is used only by a count assertion and by the 'uncompilable for an unlisted syntax rule' filter. The generator that exists to reach shapes nobody enumerated never feeds the assertion the contract is stated in.
failure: No live defect - I ran the missing assertion myself. Two campaigns (160k random META-alphabet sources, then 100k sources composed from 40 realistic regex fragments; 63,286 accepted-and-compilable) matched against six 64-char adversarial inputs produced zero matches over 20 ms. The failure is in the suite: a leak reachable only by a generated shape would be counted as covered by ALL_CANDIDATES's existence while never being timed. sampleSources' seed is fixed and its length band is 4-8, which cannot even mint a chained blowup, so today's 30k sources are frozen in a region where the expensive assertion would find nothing anyway.
remediation: Attach the bounded-time assertion to the accepted subset of ALL_CANDIDATES, not only CORPUS. Keep wall-clock manageable by timing the aggregate rather than per-source: for each accepted source run inputsFor(src), assert the total elapsed for the sweep is under a budget, with a per-source guard recording the worst offender so a failure names it. My run of 63k accepted sources x 6 inputs finished in 3.8 s, comfortably inside the file's 60 s timeout.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "a generated corpus feeds the cheap assertions and not the expensive one". Assert that the set of sources the timing sweep consumed is a superset of the accepted members of ALL_CANDIDATES - derived, so adding a new generator (a fourth sampleSources call, a new template family) automatically extends the sweep instead of silently joining the count-only path. Widen the generator at the same time: add a 9-25 length band to sampleSources, which is where my structured-fragment run showed the accepted-but-nearly-hostile region lives.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: inputsFor(src) at regex-safety.test.ts:156, which caps every input at MAX_MATCH_INPUT - the same clamp Allowlist.has applies, so the timed inputs stay the ones a caller can actually reach. Also relies on isRedosSafeSource being cheap on the 40k rejected sources; my run screened 160k in 551 ms.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none today. It would redden if a generated source ever exceeds the budget, which is the intent.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found - I ran the equivalent sweep (an added probe file, since removed) over 260k generated sources and it came back clean, so attaching it should not redden the current tree. The risk I did not measure is CI wall-clock under contention: the file's own header records a 50 ms per-match budget flaking at 59-81 ms under full-suite CPU load, which is why PER_MATCH_BUDGET_MS is 500; an aggregate budget over 60k sources needs the same generosity or it becomes a flake generator rather than a screen.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied and a leak exists that only a length-9+ generated source reaches, the current sampleSources band (4-8) still cannot mint it, so widening the band matters as much as attaching the assertion. Attaching it alone would make the suite slower without extending reach.

summary: matchGlob has zero production callers - `grep -rn matchGlob packages examples --include=*.ts` returns only its own definition, identity-filter.test.ts and stated-bounds.test.ts. Its JSDoc says so: "exported for its own unit tests". It is also not merely a widened surface but a semantically different door onto the same policy: filterHandles('') means keep-all, while matchGlob('', v) matches only the empty string. identity-filter.test.ts:150 calls it "a second door onto the same policy, so it owes the same verdicts" and then filters '' out of the parity rows - the one input where the two doors disagree is the one the parity table declines to grade.
failure: An in-package caller (or a future list-users variant) that reaches for the documented primitive rather than the wrapper - matchGlob(filter, handle) with the filter the parley_list_users schema accepts, which permits '' because it has .max() and no .min() - gets an empty roster for a client that serialised an unset filter as ''. That is exactly the answer identity-filter.ts:71's own doc says must never be how an omitted filter reads: "the one answer a caller cannot tell apart from a real outage - an empty roster - is never how an omitted or an illegal filter reads." The wrapper honours that rule; the exported primitive does not.
remediation: Make globMatch/matchGlob module-private and have identity-filter.test.ts reach the walk through filterHandles (which it already does for the roster-verdict table). If the exhaustive reference-matcher corpus genuinely needs the raw primitive, keep the export but move the empty-filter normalisation into it so both doors answer identically, and delete the "exported for its own unit tests" clause - a symbol exported for tests is a symbol the next in-package caller will use.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "a module exports two entry points onto one policy that disagree on an input the schema admits", not this pair. Parameterize the existing ROSTER_INPUTS table over BOTH doors with no row exclusions: every input the parley_list_users schema accepts (including '' and every length up to MAX_GLOB_LEN) must produce the same verdict through filterHandles and through whatever primitive the module exports. Today that case fails on the '' row, which is the finding; after the fix it passes and locks the agreement. Add a companion case asserting no symbol in identity-filter.ts is exported without a non-test caller, derived by scanning src for importers rather than listing names.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: filterHandles' `if (filter === undefined || filter === '') return items;` at identity-filter.ts:77 - the branch that encodes the empty-means-unset rule, and the branch the primitive lacks. Also relies on transport/list-users-tool.ts:128 calling filterHandles(users, filter) and nothing else, which I verified by grep.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: If the export is kept and normalised instead of removed: matchGlob('', 'anything') would newly return true, where today it returns false.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: Removing the export breaks identity-filter.test.ts's two matchGlob describes (about 1,400 generated assertions in 'agrees with an exhaustive reference matcher', plus the semantics table and the 'matchGlob: $label is $verdict' rows) and stated-bounds.test.ts's 'glob filter length ceiling (MAX_GLOB_LEN)' probe at line 64 and its CAPACITIES row at line 202, both of which call matchGlob directly. That is substantial rework, and the exhaustive reference-matcher case is the most valuable test in the file; losing it to close a surface nobody calls would be a bad trade. The normalise-instead-of-remove variant breaks only the rows assuming literal-empty semantics - I did not enumerate which, and I did not run either variant.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Neither variant fixes a live defect: no production path calls matchGlob today, so the divergence is latent. If applied while the real concern is the roster's empty-answer ambiguity, it changes nothing a user sees. I report it as a surface/astonishment issue, and the honest weighing is that the removal variant costs more test value than the divergence currently costs.

summary: createRemoteHttpApp never calls hardenErrorSurface, so any failure raised by Express itself (body parser) bypasses handlePost's try/catch and reaches Express's default handler, which renders err.stack — absolute install paths and frame list — into the response body, and logs nothing for the operator. The two auth front doors harden this; the third, publicly exported, factory does not.
failure: POST /mcp with content-type: application/json and body '{"jsonrpc":' on an app built by createRemoteHttpApp(plugin, cfg, { insecureNoAuth: true }) -> HTTP 400 with an HTML body: 'SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input at parse (/tmp/careening/worktrees/core-engine/node_modules/body-parser/lib/types/json.js:91:21) ...'. Reproduced. Two further defects in the same response: it is HTML, not the JSON-RPC envelope every other error path on this endpoint returns, and console.error is never called, so the operator sees nothing. Same for an oversized body (413) and a bad content-encoding.
remediation: Call hardenErrorSurface(app) at the end of createRemoteHttpApp, after app.post/get/delete are mounted. Traced: adding `import { hardenErrorSurface } from '../auth/error-surface.js';` plus `hardenErrorSurface(app);` after the DELETE mount turns the body above into a text/plain '400 Bad Request' with the error logged to stderr. Consider moving error-surface.ts out of auth/ since transport/ now depends on it (no cycle today: error-surface.ts imports only node:http and express types).

Drive auth/error-surface.test.ts's FRONT_DOORS from every exported app factory rather than a hand-written list — enumerate the `create*App` exports in index.ts and require each to answer every TRIGGER with a body that contains neither 'Error:' nor a filesystem path nor 'node_modules', across all three BOOT_ENVS. Add the plain reactive door as a row today. Existing test too narrow: http-gating.test.ts's '500 path hides internal detail' spies StreamableHTTPServerTransport.prototype.handleRequest, i.e. only errors that reach a Parley handler.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: auth/error-surface.ts hardenErrorSurface: `app.set('env','production'); app.use(terminalErrorHandler)`, and terminalErrorHandler's `if (res.headersSent) { next(err); return; }` branch, which keeps an already-streaming MCP response intact.

remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none by status; bodies change: a framework-level 400/413 becomes text/plain '400 Bad Request' instead of HTML+stack, and app env=production disables Express's development-only `json spaces: 2` pretty-printing on JSON responses.

In particular http-gating.test.ts's method GRID (PUT 404 comes from finalhandler, not from an error) and the auth doors' own double hardenErrorSurface call are unaffected.

summary: FRONT_DOORS is a hand-written array whose own comment claims 'Every front door hardenErrorSurface is applied to ... A control applied in one factory and forgotten in the next is invisible unless the matrix is driven from this list'. The list names two of the three exported app factories; createRemoteHttpApp is absent, which is precisely why the control is missing there. The matrix is 3 envs x 5 triggers x 2 doors and cannot fail for the door that lacks the control.

Replace the literal array with a derivation plus a membership floor, and add a self-check row that a door known NOT to be hardened fails the matrix (build a bare express app in the test and assert the matrix rejects it) — otherwise the derivation can silently grade zero doors. The same shape applies to any future control (rate limiting, security headers) audited per-factory.

summary: The live-push topic guard uses the EXPLICIT subscribed set (`subscribed.has(m.topic)`), never the post/fetch set. summary: The ReDoS/CPU budget table grades security behaviour with `performance.now()` deltas against fixed millisecond ceilings (CPU_BUDGET_MS = 500) and with a relative timing comparison (`matchCost(WORST) > matchCost('ctx-literal')`). summary: evictionCandidate's second pass reads from the NEWEST end on the premise that the owner's registration is "necessarily the oldest". When the owner's connector registers AFTER an anonymous flood — the ordinary case, since Claude does DCR at connect time — the owner IS the newest, and while they hold only a pending consent (ownerApproved:false by design) the next attacker registration deletes their registration out from under the consent page they are typing into.
failure: Register 100 clients, each calling /authorize so it holds one live pending consent. The owner's connector then registers (evicting one flood client, becoming the newest entry in `clients`) and opens /authorize. The flood registers one more client_id: `anyState` covers all 100, `approved` is empty, so `[...ids].reverse().find(id => !approved.has(id))` returns the owner's client_id and `clients.delete` removes it. completeConsent still mints a code (it never consults `clients`), and /token then answers invalid_client via the SDK's clientsStore lookup. The owner spends the passphrase and gets nothing, repeatably. Reproduced: with a test written exactly this way, `p.clientsStore.getClient('owner-claude')` is `undefined` — "owner registration evicted: expected undefined to be defined".
remediation: Stop trying to solve this with an ordering — I traced that no single ordering can: MRU (today) loses the 'owner arrives during a flood' case, and LRU loses the 'owner arrives before a flood' case that oauth-provider.test.ts already covers. Change the accounting instead: give registrations whose ONLY live state is anonymous (a pending consent) their own sub-budget, e.g. floor(MAX_CLIENTS/2). Shed within that sub-tier (newest-first, as now) when it is over budget, so the first, stateless-victim pass of evictionCandidate always has a candidate for an arriving registration and the second pass can never reach a registration that has just been created.
testUpgrade: The class is 'the owner's mid-consent state is evicted because the flood's timing relative to the owner differs from the one row the table encodes'. In oauth-provider.test.ts's `an anonymous flood never displaces state the owner is mid-way through creating`, widen ARRIVALS from ['before','after'] to ['before','after','during'], where 'during' runs the flood, seeds the owner mid-consent, and then runs MORE flood before calling ownerStillWorks() — i.e. parameterize on when the flood runs relative to the owner's whole consent TRANSACTION, not relative to their arrival. Generate the flood length as MAX_CLIENTS + k for k in {0,1,5} so a cap that binds only exactly at the boundary is also caught.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: evictionCandidate's existing first pass, `ids.find((id) => !anyState.has(id))`, which must keep returning a stateless registration — that is the branch the sub-budget exists to keep populated; and ParleyOAuthProvider.clientStates(), whose `ownerApproved: false` yield for `pending` is what identifies the anonymous tier.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: The 51st concurrent anonymous client_id that tries to hold a pending consent would have its registration shed earlier than today (it is refused a slot it currently gets), so a legitimate deployment with >50 simultaneous distinct connectors mid-consent would see registrations churn.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I checked the two assertions the existing CELLS rows make, `expect(peek(p)[capped.store].size).toBe(capped.size)` and ownerStillWorks(); the sub-budget evicts within `clients` rather than refusing, so clients.size still settles at MAX_CLIENTS. I did not implement it, so this is reasoning over those two assertions, not an observed run.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while the ordering bug remains, the owner is still evictable in any window where the anonymous sub-tier is saturated by 50 distinct clients AND the owner is the newest — so the sub-budget must replace the reliance on ordering, not sit beside it.

summary: MODE_ONLY_OPTIONS is the thing under test, and invariants.test.ts:481 builds its row set by regexing MODE_ONLY_OPTIONS out of the same file. summary: The guard titled 'the auth layer escapes at every interpolation of every page it renders, reachable or not' only treats a template literal as a page when it matches `/<!doctype|<\/[a-z]+>/i`. A fragment built entirely from void elements or attributes is not recognised, so its unescaped interpolations are never graded — the guard's promise is exactly that unreachability is no excuse, and this is a whole shape it never looks at.

summary: issue() always writes `scope: scopes.join(' ')`, so a grant with no scopes emits `"scope": ""`. RFC 6749 §5.1's `scope = scope-token *( SP scope-token )` has no empty production; the field must be omitted. The package already reasons carefully about this elsewhere — namedScopes() drops empty tokens on the way IN — but re-introduces one on the way out.

SDK sets params.scopes undefined → completeConsent stores `scopes: []` → issue([]) → the /token response body is `{"access_token":"...","token_type":"bearer","expires_in":3600,"refresh_token":"...","scope":""}`. A client validating `scope` against the ABNF, or splitting it without a `.filter(Boolean)`, sees a grant for one scope named the empty string.
remediation: In issue(), replace `scope: scopes.join(' ')` with `...(scopes.length > 0 ? { scope: scopes.join(' ') } : {})`.

Parameterize the existing CONSENTED_SCOPES rows in oauth-provider.test.ts over the RAW response object rather than a normalized set: for each row assert `Object.hasOwn(tokens, 'scope') === (scopes.length > 0)` and, when present, `/^\S+( \S+)*$/.test(tokens.scope)`. Apply the same raw-shape assertion to remote.test.ts's SCOPE_ROWS, whose `scopeSet()` helper (`String(scope).split(' ').filter(Boolean)`) currently normalizes exactly this away.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: OAuthTokens from the SDK, whose `scope` is already optional in OAuthTokensSchema (`scope: z.string().optional()`), so omitting the key type-checks and parses.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — this is an emit-side change only.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: Two, traced: oauth-provider.test.ts:574 `code exchange of a consent for [] grants exactly those` and its twin at :588 for the refresh grant both assert `expect(tokens.scope).toBe(scopes.join(' '))`, which for the `[]` row of CONSENTED_SCOPES is `expect(undefined).toBe('')`. remote.test.ts's `an empty scope parameter`/`a lone space` rows survive, because scopeSet(undefined) is `new Set(['undefined'])`… actually `String(undefined).split(' ')` yields ['undefined'], so those two rows WOULD also fail and need the raw-shape assertion above.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing else stays broken; the inbound namedScopes() filter is independent and already correct.

summary: hashOwnerSecret rejects only the empty string. The owner passphrase is the sole gate that authorizes the whole bridge on a public origin, and the only brute-force control is a per-IP 10-per-15-minutes limiter on /parley/consent — so total guesses across addresses are unbounded. Every other boot-time invariant in this package fails fast on a weak configuration (trust proxy true, a blank oidc gate, a non-literal mcpPath); this one does not.

A caller with 200 source addresses gets 2000 guesses per 15 minutes against a keyspace of ~95, with no boot warning and no server-side signal that anything is wrong.

Parameterize a corpus over the boundary rather than pinning one string: `['', ' ', '\t', 'x', 'x'.repeat(MIN-1)]` must all throw and `['x'.repeat(MIN), a long passphrase]` must all round-trip, with MIN read from the exported constant so the table cannot drift from the guard. The existing `rejects a malformed stored hash and an empty passphrase` row is too narrow to have caught this: it only asserts `hashOwnerSecret('')` throws.

remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Any passphrase shorter than the chosen floor, including one an existing deployment is already using via PARLEY_OWNER_PASSPHRASE — that deployment fails to boot after upgrade. PARLEY_OWNER_SECRET_HASH deployments are unaffected, because makeOwnerVerifier never sees the plaintext.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found at a floor of 8 — I checked every passphrase literal in the auth tests: GOOD_PASS 'open sesame', OWNER_PASS/PASS 'correct horse battery staple', 'correct horse', and 'any passphrase at all' are all ≥ 8; the negative cases assert rejection anyway. examples/self-host-remote/test/builtin-only-options.test.ts uses 'hunter2' (7 chars) as an env value but, from its name, only checks option routing — I did not run it under a floor of 8, so a floor of 8 needs that file re-checked; a floor of 6 clears it.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Distributed guessing stays open: a floor raises the cost of the keyspace but does not bound total attempts, because the limiter keys on req.ip by design. If the threat is a botnet, this fix alone does not close it.

summary: `RemoteAuthServer = OAuthRemoteServer | OidcRemoteServer`. The builtin variant's close() is TERMINAL (it drops issued credentials, stops the sweeper and shuts the limiter stores down, and a later listen() throws), while the oidc variant inherits RemoteHttpServer's documented idempotent-and-re-listenable close(). A composition root holding a RemoteAuthServer cannot tell which it has, and the type says nothing — teardown.test.ts has to carry a hand-written 'terminal' | 're-listenable' field per factory precisely because the value does not carry it.

testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a union whose variants differ in a lifecycle contract nothing on the value expresses'. Rewrite teardown.test.ts's Factory.afterClose so the expected verdict is READ OFF THE RETURNED SERVER rather than hand-written per row — the row then fails the day a new factory's contract disagrees with what its value advertises, instead of the day someone remembers to add a row.

remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — additive.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — teardown.test.ts's FACTORIES rows would keep passing with their literal afterClose values until the testUpgrade above replaces them.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: A discriminant does not make the builtin close() re-listenable; it only makes the difference visible. If the real goal is one contract, the fix is instead to re-arm the sweeper and fresh limiter stores in listen(), which is a larger change and would newly accept a listen-after-close that today throws.

summary: When the bounded WAL-conversion retry gives up, `applyPragmas` breaks out of the loop and then unconditionally executes `PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL`. The connection therefore runs in rollback-journal mode with the reduced-sync setting that SQLite only certifies as corruption-safe in WAL mode, and it never re-attempts the conversion for the rest of its (process-lifetime) existence. One stderr line is the entire signal; nothing appears in `subscriptionHealth()` and nothing retries.
failure: Reproduced: hold `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` on a fresh file from a second connection, then `openDriver(path, { busyTimeoutMs: 100 })`. Output: `WAL conversion still busy after 20 retries; continuing in default journal mode`, then `PRAGMA journal_mode` -> `delete` and `PRAGMA synchronous` -> `1`. After the peer commits and a third bridge converts the file to WAL, the degraded connection still reports `delete` and `synchronous=1` — it never re-probes. For the whole life of that bridge process, readers block the writer (the property DESIGN §9/§10 rests on for multi-process safety) and the store is written with synchronous=NORMAL outside WAL.
remediation: Track whether the conversion succeeded and gate the sync downgrade on it: `let wal = false;` set to `true` on the successful `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL`, and `if (wal) driver.exec('PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL');`. That alone leaves the connection permanently in FULL sync even after the file becomes WAL, so also re-probe the conversion (cheapest place: the existing background cadence, or on the first lock-classed poll failure) and record the degraded state somewhere `subscriptionHealth()` or connect()'s caller can read, rather than only on stderr.
testUpgrade: The class is "a fallback path leaves a safety-relevant setting configured for the precondition it just abandoned". Parameterize the existing `openDriver concurrent first-boot WAL race` case in src/driver.test.ts into a table over `{walConverts: true|false}` that, for BOTH arms, reads back EVERY pragma the cross-process story names — journal_mode, busy_timeout, synchronous — and asserts the tuple, reusing driver-parity.test.ts's `PRAGMAS` list so a pragma added later is graded on the degraded arm too. Today the degrade case asserts only "did not throw" plus the warning line, and driver-parity's read-back only ever runs on an uncontended fresh file, so no test observes the degraded connection's settings at all.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `applyPragmas` in src/driver.ts — specifically the `break;` after `driver.exec('PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL')` (the success exit) and the `break;` inside `if (i >= WAL_RETRIES)` (the degrade exit); the fix sets the flag only on the first. It also relies on `classifyDbError(e) !== 'lock' -> throw e` still routing every non-contention failure out before the degrade exit is reachable.

remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none. The degraded open still succeeds and still returns a usable driver, exactly as today.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I applied the fix and ran the whole package: 635/635 green. I specifically checked driver-parity.test.ts's `reads back every pragma the cross-process story rests on` (expects synchronous=1) — it opens a fresh uncontended file where WAL converts, so it stays green; and src/driver.test.ts's WAL-race table, which asserts no-throw, attempt counts and the warning line, none of which move.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: It closes the integrity half only. If applied while the rest of the bug remains, the connection still never re-attempts the WAL conversion, so it keeps rollback-journal locking semantics — readers blocking the writer for peer bridges — for its whole lifetime, and the only notice is still one stderr line an MCP stdio host routinely discards. It also introduces a new silent state: a connection stuck at synchronous=FULL long after the file became WAL, i.e. a permanent throughput penalty with nothing reporting it. That is why the remediation above is two parts, not one.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The degrade is reached only when another opener holds the write lock across all 20 retries (~290 ms of Atomics.wait). Two callers on the new path: two bridges both opening a fresh file concurrently — one wins the conversion and sets `wal = true`, the loser degrades and skips the downgrade; neither writes shared state, `wal` is a local of `applyPragmas`, so the orderings are independent. A third opener arriving after the lock is released converts the file to WAL regardless of what the degraded connection cached (verified: `third journal_mode` -> `wal`).

summary: The Cross-process safety section states that "Every connection opens with `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL`, `PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000`, and `PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL` … readers never block the writer", and that `synchronous = NORMAL`'s price is that a committed transaction "can be lost on power loss … (the file itself is never corrupted — this is a durability trade, not an integrity one)". Both sentences are unconditional; the code ships a branch on which neither holds. SQLite's own documentation scopes the corruption-freedom of synchronous=NORMAL to WAL mode ("probably DELETE mode is safe too on modern filesystems" is the strongest it says otherwise), and in rollback-journal mode readers demonstrably do block the writer.
failure: A reader of the README concludes the store cannot be corrupted and that peers never block each other. remediation: Scope the sentences to the WAL case and name the degrade: state that the conversion is bounded-retried, that a first-boot race can leave a connection in the default journal mode, what that costs (readers block the writer; synchronous=NORMAL is not certified corruption-safe outside WAL — which is why the F1 fix leaves it at FULL there), and how an operator detects it (the `WAL conversion still busy` stderr line).

summary: `classifyDbError` reaches its decision from `code` OR `message`, but ERROR_SPECS pairs every code with the canonical SQLite message that matches the same arm, and ERROR_SHAPES only varies which of the two is populated — never sets them in conflict. So the `code` arm is graded by nothing: deleting `/BUSY|LOCKED/.test(code) ||` from src/classify.ts leaves all 635 tests green. The file's own JSDoc anticipates the mirror-image gap (message arms un-exercised) and closes it with the node:sqlite shape, but the `code` half was left with no counterpart.
failure: Mutation applied and verified applied: `if (/BUSY|LOCKED/.test(code) || /database is locked|database table is locked/i.test(msg))` -> `if (/database is locked|database table is locked/i.test(msg))`. Result: `Test Files 19 passed (19), Tests 635 passed (635)`. Any SQLite contention condition whose errmsg is not one of those two literals — an extended BUSY/LOCKED code, or a message-text change in a future SQLite — then classifies as `unavailable`, which per the README's own rule means a stderr line per topic per minute for the one class it promises is silent. Separately, on the node:sqlite fallback the classifier reads only `code` (always the useless `ERR_SQLITE_ERROR`) and `message`, while the error also carries the authoritative numeric `errcode` (verified: `{ code: 'ERR_SQLITE_ERROR', errcode: 5, errstr: 'database is locked' }` for a real contended write) that nothing consults.
remediation: Split the fixture's two dimensions: give ERROR_SPECS an explicit `message`/`code` pair per row plus at least one row where they disagree (a BUSY-family code with a non-canonical message, and a benign code with a message containing `no such table`), so each arm decides at least one row alone. In src/classify.ts, also read node:sqlite's numeric `errcode` (5 SQLITE_BUSY, 6 SQLITE_LOCKED, 11 SQLITE_CORRUPT, 26 SQLITE_NOTADB, plus their extended forms via `errcode & 0xff`) before falling back to message text, so the fallback driver is classified on a code rather than on prose.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS — "a table whose rows co-vary two inputs of a decision function, so either input can be deleted green". Make ERROR_SPECS a cross product of `{codeSignal}` x `{messageSignal}` (matching / non-matching / absent) with the expected class per cell, and add a negative-control case asserting that for each arm there exists at least one row the OTHER arm cannot decide — a property assertion over the table, so a future row that re-collapses the dimensions fails immediately. The same generator should drive test/driver-parity.test.ts's PROVOCATIONS so the driver-raised errors are checked against the same cells.

summary: `normalizeMillis` accepts any positive safe integer, but `connect_timeout_ms` is handed straight to `setTimeout` inside `withDeadline` (and to node-redis' `socket.connectTimeout`). Node truncates a delay above 2^31-1 to 1ms, so the LARGEST accepted timeouts become the SHORTEST — and the resulting error blames the network while quoting the very value that caused it.
failure: `connect({ url: 'redis://127.0.0.1:6390', connect_timeout_ms: 2147483648 })` against a healthy, reachable Redis rejects after 8ms with `parley-redis: cannot reach 127.0.0.1:6390 (connect_timeout_ms=2147483648)` (reproduced; Node prints `TimeoutOverflowWarning: ... Timeout duration was set to 1`). Same root breaks `subscribe()` and the long-poll, whose `connectReader` uses the same `withDeadline`. `failure-modes.test.ts` ("does not bound a handshake that never completes — withDeadline does") treats that deadline as the load-bearing bound, so this inverts the one mechanism the suite says is holding.
remediation: Give `normalizeMillis` an upper bound for knobs that become a timer delay: reject `connect_timeout_ms` above 2_147_483_647 with the same key-naming message (`must be a positive whole number of milliseconds no greater than 2147483647`). `block_ms` needs no bound — it is a server-side `XREAD BLOCK` argument, not a timer — so bound the two knobs separately rather than widening one shared validator. Clamping inside `withDeadline` instead is the quieter alternative but contradicts this package's reject-don't-coerce discipline.
testUpgrade: The CLASS is "a validated numeric knob whose accepted range is wider than the range its consumer can represent". `test/config-fixtures.ts` already tables `connect_timeout_ms` rejections and jumps from `1.5` straight to `2 ** 53` — the whole band between `2**31` and `2**53` is untested. Add a generated boundary row set per ms knob, derived from the consumer's ceiling rather than hand-picked: `[TIMER_MAX - 1 (accepted), TIMER_MAX (accepted), TIMER_MAX + 1 (rejected), 2**53 (rejected)]` where `TIMER_MAX = 2**31 - 1`, and pair it with a live-server row asserting that every ACCEPTED `connect_timeout_ms` still connects successfully against a reachable endpoint — that arm is what catches an inverted knob rather than merely a widened one, and it would also catch any future knob routed to a timer.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `normalizeMillis`'s existing guard `if (typeof value !== 'number' || !Number.isSafeInteger(value) || value <= 0)` and its `pluginError(...)` message template naming the key; the `describeValue` renderer for the rejected value.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `connect_timeout_ms: 2147483648` (and anything larger) — today accepted and then silently behaving as 1ms.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found in the rows I read: `test/config-fixtures.ts` `rejectedByKnob.connect_timeout_ms` tops out at `2 ** 53` (already rejected, stays rejected); `test/live-config.test.ts` `it.each(CONFIG_KEYS)('connect() accepts %s set to null')` uses null. I did NOT read `test/knob-effects.test.ts`'s full WireEffect value table, so a row there using a huge non-default `connect_timeout_ms` to prove the knob reaches `socket.connectTimeout` could break — that is the one place to check before applying.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: It fixes only this package's connect knob. If the same overflow class exists on any other ms knob routed to `setTimeout` (in core's `catchup.block_max_ms` path or another plugin), those stay broken; and it does not give an operator a way to express "effectively no connect timeout", which is presumably what a >24-day value was reaching for.

failure: Reproduced: `const p = plugin.post(t, handle, 'x'); plugin.disconnect();` rejects with exactly `parley-redis: Disconnects client (topic 'z11-2-i2x7is', key 'parleytest:0ysl15:z11-2-i2x7is')`. This is reachable in normal operation — SIGTERM reaches `cli.ts`'s `shutdown` -> `bridge.shutdown()` -> `plugin.disconnect()` while a `parley_post` tool call is in flight — and core renders a thrown seam error into the model's context, so the agent is told 'Disconnects client'. Every neighbouring path in this package (`require()`, `unreachable()`, `openCommandClient`, the STOPPED/DEGRADED lines) goes to real trouble to name the cause; this one does not.
remediation: In `labelled`, recognise node-redis' lifecycle errors by `err.name` (`DisconnectsClientError` / `ClientClosedError` / `ClientOfflineError`) — matching the name rather than importing a deep dist path, which is not part of node-redis' public surface — and substitute a plugin-authored sentence, e.g. `parley-redis: the connection was closed while this call was in flight (topic '…', key '…'); the bridge is shutting down or reconnecting`. Keep the topic/key suffix and the `fromServer` sanitization for every other error unchanged.
testUpgrade: The CLASS is "an error text this plugin did not write reaching the operator and the model unexplained". `hostile-server.test.ts` grades what the SERVER says; nothing grades what the CLIENT LIBRARY says. Add a table over the library's lifecycle errors — driven by actually racing the calls, not by constructing the errors — `[post, fetchRecent, fetchRecent-with-blockMs, subscribe] x [disconnect() in flight, call issued after disconnect(), call issued during a reconnect]`, asserting for every cell that the rejection matches `/^parley-redis: /`, names the topic and the key, and does NOT match a deny-list of the library's own fragments (`/Disconnects client|The client is closed|The client is offline/`). The deny-list is the part that generalises: a node-redis upgrade adding a new lifecycle error fails the table instead of shipping another fragment.

summary: `new Pool({ connectionString, max })` sets no `connectionTimeoutMillis`, so `connect()`'s bootstrap checkout waits forever on a peer that completes the TCP handshake and then never speaks. Every other wait in this plugin is deliberately bounded (LOCK_WAIT_MS, LISTENER_WAIT_MS, and listener.ts:9 says so in as many words), and this is the one that is not — it is also the first call any bridge makes.
failure: Reproduced: a `net.createServer` on 127.0.0.1:15999 that accepts and holds the socket; `new PostgresPlugin().connect({url:'postgres://parley:parley@127.0.0.1:15999/parley'})` was still pending after 8000ms (`settleWithin` -> 'hung'). In production this is a firewalled port, a stuck pgbouncer, or a failing-over primary: `createStdioBridge` never returns, the MCP host sees a server that never initialises, and there is no diagnostic on stderr.
remediation: Pass `connectionTimeoutMillis` to both `new Pool(...)` (index.ts:90) and `new Client(...)` (listener.ts:53). It must be strictly greater than `LOCK_WAIT_MS` (5000) because on a Pool this option bounds the whole acquire, including queueing behind `pool_size` busy clients — a `post()` waiting out its 5s `lock_timeout` holds a checkout for that long, and a shorter connect timeout would turn documented lock contention into acquire failures. Alternatively, take the bootstrap on a dedicated `Client` rather than a pool checkout, so the connect bound and the acquire bound stay separate knobs.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a seam entry point that waits on a socket with no ceiling'. Add a table-driven case parameterized over {entry point} x {stall shape}: entry points = connect / post / fetchRecent / subscribe / disconnect; stall shapes = a `net` server that accepts and never writes, and a `net` proxy that forwards the handshake and then stops forwarding. Every cell asserts the call settles (resolved or rejected, either is fine) inside a stated budget via `settleWithin`, and that the rejection names `parley-postgres:`. That generator would also catch a future path that dials without a bound. The existing connection-hygiene.test.ts is too narrow because every one of its cells runs against a healthy server that closes sockets promptly, and listener-blackout.test.ts's MockClient.connect() throws immediately rather than hanging, so neither can reach this arm.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: pg's ConnectionParameters `connectionTimeoutMillis` (pg-pool rejects the acquire with 'timeout exceeded when trying to connect'); and the existing catch at index.ts:105-111 which already does `this.starting.delete(pool)` + `pool.end()` on a bootstrap failure — but only for failures raised INSIDE the try, which the checkout at line 98 is not (see the separate starting-set finding).
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A `connect()` against a server whose handshake legitimately takes longer than the chosen budget (TLS on a loaded box, a pgbouncer under a connection storm) now fails where it previously blocked and eventually succeeded. On the Pool, additionally, a `post()` issued while all `pool_size` connections are checked out and waiting on their 5s lock_timeout would reject with a pg acquire-timeout string if the budget is set below LOCK_WAIT_MS.

I did not run the suite with the fix applied, so this is reasoning from reading, not a measurement.

summary: No `query_timeout` and no `keepAlive` are set on the Pool or the listener Client, so when a peer stops responding without sending FIN or RST every in-flight query never settles — and `disconnect()`, which awaits `pool.end()` and `listener.end()`, inherits that. `pg-pool.end()` resolves only once every checked-out client is released, and the client is blocked on a query that will never answer, so shutdown never completes.
failure: Reproduced through a `net` proxy on 127.0.0.1:15996 forwarding to a real postgres: connect and a first post succeed; the proxy then stops forwarding in both directions (no FIN, no RST). `plugin.post(topic, 'u', 'after')` -> 'hung' after 12000ms, and `plugin.disconnect()` -> 'hung' after a further 12000ms. cli.ts:28-33 wires SIGINT/SIGTERM to `bridge.shutdown().finally(() => process.exit(0))`, so the bridge process ignores SIGTERM indefinitely and only SIGKILL removes it.
remediation: Set `query_timeout` on the pool/client config (client-side, so it fires even when no bytes come back — `statement_timeout` cannot help here because the server's reply is what is lost) at a value comfortably above LOCK_WAIT_MS, and enable `keepAlive` with a `keepAliveInitialDelayMillis` so the OS surfaces a dead peer as an error instead of silence. Separately, bound `disconnect()`: race each `end()` against a deadline and proceed once it expires, so teardown returns even when a socket cannot be closed gracefully.
testUpgrade: Same generator as the connect-hang class, extended with the mid-session stall shape: a `net` proxy that forwards the handshake, then stops forwarding, parameterized over {post, fetchRecent(since), fetchRecent(blockMs), subscribe, disconnect} x {stall before the call, stall during the call}. Every cell asserts settlement inside a budget. Add one dedicated cell asserting `disconnect()` settles while a query is stalled, since that is the one with an operational consequence (SIGTERM ignored). teardown-races-setup.test.ts is too narrow to catch this: its `MockClient.end()` and `FakePool.end()` both resolve as soon as `outstanding` hits zero, so no cell there can model a socket that will not close.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: pg Client's `query_timeout` option (rejects the in-flight query and destroys the connection), and pg-pool's `end()` contract that it settles once checked-out clients are released — which a rejected query does satisfy, because post()'s `finally { client.release(); }` at index.ts:231-233 runs on the rejection path.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A legitimately slow query is now aborted. The one at risk in this package is the retention DELETE: PRUNE_BATCH is 5000 rows per statement, which on a cold table with a slow disk can exceed a few seconds. A `query_timeout` below that turns the first prune after enabling retention into a permanent no-op (each tick aborts and the swallowed catch at index.ts:161 retries forever). Also, a `post()` genuinely waiting out its full 5s `lock_timeout` would be killed by the client instead of by the server unless the timeout exceeds LOCK_WAIT_MS, which would replace the named `parley-postgres: gave up after 5000ms waiting for the write lock…` message with a raw driver string — exactly what errors.ts:90-101 exists to prevent.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I looked at retention.test.ts (the 5001-row and 15001-row backlog cells, which take seconds of real DELETE time and are the ones most exposed to a query_timeout that is set too low) and lock-wait.test.ts 'connect() gives up on a held bootstrap lock instead of hanging' (which asserts the 55P03 message, so it would go red if the client timeout beat the server's lock_timeout). I did not run either with the fix applied.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Bounding `disconnect()` alone without the query timeout would let shutdown return while a live socket is still attached to a stopped plugin — precisely the orphan connection-hygiene.test.ts exists to forbid. The two halves have to land together, or the fix trades a hang for a leak.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Two callers on the new path: a `post()` whose query_timeout fires concurrently with a `disconnect()` already awaiting `pool.end()`. The rejection releases the client, pool.end() then resolves, and post()'s catch runs `client.query('ROLLBACK')` on a released client — which rejects, is swallowed by `.catch(() => undefined)` at index.ts:229, and then `lockWaitAbandoned` rethrows the original. That ordering is safe. The reverse — disconnect's deadline expiring first and the query answering afterwards — lands in a stopped lifecycle guarded by `epoch`.

summary: `ensureListener` memoises the dial in `this.listenerPromise` and clears it only from `createListener().catch(...)`. A dial that never SETTLES therefore pins the memo forever: `withDeadline` rejects the caller at 5000ms but leaves the memo in place, so every later `subscribe` and every native long-poll awaits the same dead promise and times out again — permanently, even after the network has healed. The error it hands back says the opposite of what is true.
failure: Reproduced: connect through a `net` proxy on 127.0.0.1:15997, flip the proxy to black-hole new connections, `subscribe('t1')` rejects with `parley-postgres: could not establish the live path for topic 't1' — the listener connection did not come up within 5000ms. … a retry succeeds once the database is reachable again.` Restore forwarding, wait 200ms, `subscribe('t2')` rejects with the identical message. Push is dead for the whole process lifetime and the error text asserts the retry that cannot work. Core's push loop rethrows a non-NoSuchTopicError, so the bridge fails to come up and stays failed.
remediation: In `ensureListener`, when `withDeadline` rejects, clear `this.listenerPromise` if it still points at the timed-out attempt AND end the abandoned dial, then let the next call start a fresh one. Ending the abandoned dial is not optional: without it, the next `subscribe` opens a second socket while the first is still in `starting`, and whichever `adoptListener` runs second overwrites `this.listener` leaving the first live and unreachable. Note that with the connect-timeout fix from the sibling finding applied, the dial rejects on its own and the existing `.catch` at listener.ts:40-43 already clears the memo — so this fix is the belt for the case where the timeout is longer than the caller's budget (`waitForNotify` passes `Math.min(blockMs, LISTENER_WAIT_MS)`, which can be as low as a few ms).
testUpgrade: The class is 'a memoised in-flight resource whose slot is only released on the settle paths that actually occur'. Parameterize a case over {how the dial ends} = {rejects fast, rejects slow, never settles} x {what the caller does next} = {retry immediately, retry after the fault clears}, asserting that after the fault clears the retry SUCCEEDS and that exactly one listener socket exists. A `never settles` arm is the row every existing file is missing. listener-blackout.test.ts is too narrow because its `MockClient.connect()` either returns or throws — `state.connectFailures` decrements and throws — so no cell there can produce a dial that hangs.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `withDeadline` (listener.ts:14-26), whose `finally` already clears the timer; and `adoptListener` (listener.ts:67-74), whose `!this.starting.delete(client)` guard is what makes an abandoned dial end itself rather than publish — but only if something removes it from `starting`, which nothing currently does outside `disconnect()`.

remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I read connection-hygiene.test.ts, which asserts `priv.listenerPromise` is undefined only AFTER `disconnect()` (line 129), and its `awaitListenerInFlight` helper spins on `listenerPromise !== undefined && listener === undefined`, a window this fix does not shorten because the memo is only cleared on the timeout path. I also read the four `reconnect` cells there and listener-blackout's nine cells; none asserts that the memo SURVIVES a timeout. I did not run the suite with the fix applied.

So this fix alone converts a permanent push outage into a permanent shutdown hang unless the abandoned dial is genuinely ended.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Two callers on the new path: subscribe A times out and clears the memo; subscribe B immediately calls ensureListener and starts dial 2; dial 1 then completes. Both clients are in `starting`, so both `adoptListener` calls succeed their `starting.delete` and the second assignment to `this.listener` orphans the first. The fix must end dial 1 at the moment it is abandoned, not rely on adoptListener to reject it.

summary: `this.starting.add(pool)` is followed by `const client = await pool.connect();` OUTSIDE the try whose catch does the `starting.delete` + `pool.end()` cleanup. A `connect()` that fails at the checkout therefore leaves its Pool in `starting` forever, violating the invariant this package's own tests assert (`starting: 0`) and growing without bound under a supervisor retry loop.
failure: Reproduced: three consecutive `plugin.connect({url:'postgres://parley:parley@127.0.0.1:1/parley'})` calls, each rejecting with ECONNREFUSED, leave `(plugin as any).starting.size === 3`. A supervisor retrying `connect()` once a second against a down database accumulates one un-ended `pg.Pool` per second until the first successful `disconnect()`.
remediation: Move the checkout inside the try. The catch cannot be reused as written — it opens with `await client.query('ROLLBACK')`, and `client` is undefined when the checkout itself is what failed, so a naive move turns an ECONNREFUSED into a TypeError. Either guard the ROLLBACK on `client !== undefined`, or add a small `catch` around the checkout alone doing `this.starting.delete(pool); await pool.end().catch(() => undefined); throw err;`.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a setup call that fails partway leaves a registry entry behind'. Extend teardown-races-setup.test.ts's ROWS table with a FAILURE dimension alongside its existing race dimension: for each await site it already names ('the pool checkout', 'the bootstrap advisory lock', 'the listener socket', 'the LISTEN'), add a row where that await REJECTS rather than being held, and assert the same registry post-condition it already asserts for the raced case — `{starting: 0, subs: 0, subscribing: 0, listens: 0, waiters: 0, pendingAborts: 0}` — plus `stillLive()` equal to zero. That generator also covers the next await someone adds before the try.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: The existing catch at index.ts:105-111: `await client.query('ROLLBACK').catch(() => undefined); client.release(); this.starting.delete(pool); await pool.end().catch(() => undefined); throw lockWaitAbandoned(...)`. Both `client.query` and `client.release` on that path assume the checkout succeeded.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none in terms of inputs; the rejection VALUE changes if the checkout error is routed through `lockWaitAbandoned`, which returns non-55P03 errors unchanged — so an ECONNREFUSED still surfaces with its original message.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I read connection-hygiene.test.ts ('subscribe-before-connect', 'post-after-disconnect', the concurrent-connect cells) and teardown-races-setup.test.ts, and no case asserts anything about `starting` after a FAILED connect; the only `starting.size` assertion is after a successful teardown. config-validation.test.ts's 'every bad value on every knob rejects within a bounded time' rejects before the pool is opened at all, so it never reaches line 98.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: It stops the unbounded growth. It does not by itself make the leaked pool harmless today — the pool holds no sockets after a failed checkout, so the only cost is memory; if the checkout hangs instead of rejecting (the connect-timeout finding), the entry is a LIVE dialing pool and `disconnect()` hangs on it.

summary: "Every wait on that lock is bounded… An unbounded wait would instead hold a pooled connection forever and take the instance's reads down with it." `SET LOCAL lock_timeout = 5000` bounds only the SERVER-side lock wait; it cannot bound a wait for bytes that never arrive. An operator reading this page concludes the failure mode described in the last sentence has been designed out, when it is reachable and I reproduced it.
failure: With the peer silent mid-session (the `net` proxy repro), `post()` holds its pooled connection indefinitely — the exact outcome the sentence says cannot happen — and with `pool_size` such posts outstanding, every read on that instance is starved, also exactly as described. The paragraph is the only place the package tells an operator what its failure envelope is.
remediation: Once the client-side timeouts land, restate the sentence to say what is actually bounded and by what: the server-side lock wait by `lock_timeout`, the dial by `connectionTimeoutMillis`, and the reply by `query_timeout`. Until then, say plainly that a peer that stops responding without closing the socket is not bounded by `lock_timeout`, so an operator can decide whether they need a TCP keepalive or a pooler in front.
testUpgrade: readme-truth.test.ts already extracts every NUMBER the README states and compares it to the export, which is why the 5000 in this paragraph is graded and the CLAIM around it is not. Extend it with a claims table whose rows pair a README assertion with the behavioural test that proves it — e.g. {'every wait on that lock is bounded' -> the settle-within table from the unbounded-wait class above}, asserting the named test file exists and that the named case id is present in it. That makes an unbacked prose guarantee a red test rather than a reviewer's catch.

summary: Two tables in this file cross a dimension with a value that makes that dimension inert, producing byte-identical duplicate cells that cost seconds each and discriminate nothing.
failure: CELLS = listenMode x waiters{1,2,3} x skewMs{0,50}; the skew is applied by `if (i > 0) await sleep(cell.skewMs * i)`, and with `waiters: 1` there is no i>0 — so `1 waiter, 0ms skew` and `1 waiter, 50ms skew` are the same run, 3 duplicate cells (one per listenMode), each budgeted 10s. TEARDOWN_CELLS = waiters{1,3} x topics{1,2} x blockMs x duringListen; the topic is `asTopic(\`t${i % cell.topics}\`)`, so with `waiters: 1` the index is always 0 and topics=1 and topics=2 are the same run — 4 more duplicate cells at 15s each. Seven cells that cannot fail independently of a sibling.
remediation: Build the tables so the inert combinations are not generated: emit the skew dimension only for `waiters > 1`, and the topics dimension only for `waiters >= topics`. Expressed as a filter on the flatMap rather than by hand-deleting rows, so a later widening of `waiters` regenerates the right cells.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a table row whose distinguishing parameter is unreachable at another parameter's value'. Add a hygiene rule to suite-hygiene.test.ts alongside its existing conditional-assertion census: for each `it.each` table in the package, assert that no two rows produce the same label-independent parameter tuple after the inert dimensions are collapsed — or, cheaper and equally effective, assert that every declared cell label is unique AND that the number of cells equals the number of distinct (parameter tuple) values the body can actually observe. That catches the next dimension someone crosses with a degenerate value.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: waiters.test.ts's own generators — `CELLS` at line 171 and `TEARDOWN_CELLS` at line 288 — and the two body expressions that consume the inert parameters (`if (i > 0) await sleep(cell.skewMs * i)` and `asTopic(\`t${i % cell.topics}\`)`).

summary: `recentWindow`'s short-circuit conflates two reasons for stopping early. When MAX_BACKFILL_PAGES (50) — not a teardown — ends the backward walk, it discards every message it did collect AND, for a since-less read (where `sinceCursor` is `undefined`), falls through `emptyWindowCursor(undefined, undefined, false)` to `asCursor(STREAM_CURSOR_PREFIX)` — the bare `@parley-stream:` that means 'the first visible event in the room'. cursor.ts's own docstring calls that value 'a position nothing observed' and throws for it on the stale path; recent-window-and-cursor.fake.test.ts's class docstring calls it 'the dangerous one'. Core persists whatever cursor it is handed, so the next start drains the room from event 0 with a fresh seen-set.
failure: shared_room mode, fake Synapse. 12 foreign events, then post 'mine-1' to topic-A, then 148 more foreign events (159 total; the 50x3 walk covers the newest 150, which includes 'mine-1'). `fetchRecent({ topic: 'topic-A', limit: 3 })` (no since) -> `{ messages: [], nextCursor: '@parley-stream:' }`. Correct answer is `{ messages: ['mine-1'], nextCursor: '$e12:fake' }` (verified: that is exactly what the code returns with the remediation applied). The README also claims the `@parley-stream:` form 'marks the timeline position the window was read AT', which is false for the tokenless value this path mints.
remediation: Split the two stop reasons. Replace the guard with `const stale = this.isStale(generation); if (collected.length < limit && !exhaustedTheTimeline && (stale || sinceCursor !== undefined)) { return { messages: [], nextCursor: emptyWindowCursor(undefined, sinceCursor, stale) }; }` and let the page-bound-with-no-since case fall through to the normal return, which already yields `collected.slice(0,limit).reverse()` and `messages.at(-1)?.cursor ?? emptyWindowCursor(tailToken, ...)`. `tailToken` is assigned from page 0's `start` before the chunk check, so a walk that completed page 0 always has an honest read position.
testUpgrade: CLASS: every reason a bounded walk can stop must map to a distinct, replayable cursor — never to a position nothing read. Extend `recent-window-and-cursor.fake.test.ts`'s SHORT_CIRCUITS table (which today holds only teardown and transport-fault rows) with a `the page bound stops the walk` row that buries `limit-1` belonging messages behind more than MAX_BACKFILL_PAGES*limit foreign events, and assert the existing invariant already written there (`drainFrom(nextCursor)` yields exactly what is still owed) plus `expect(String(nextCursor)).not.toBe('@parley-stream:')`. Parameterize over `SINCE_FORMS` x `TAIL_NOISE_DEPTHS` so the since-less and since-having arms are graded separately, and widen TAIL_NOISE_DEPTHS with a depth derived from MAX_BACKFILL_PAGES rather than a literal, so a change to the bound moves the case with it.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `emptyWindowCursor(readAt, sinceCursor, stale)` in cursor.ts — specifically the `if (readAt !== undefined) return asCursor(`${STREAM_CURSOR_PREFIX}${readAt}`)` branch, reached via `tailToken` which `recentWindow` assigns with `tailToken ??= start` BEFORE the `chunk.length === 0` check, so page 0 always sets it. Also relies on the existing tail `const nextCursor = messages.at(-1)?.cursor ?? emptyWindowCursor(tailToken, sinceCursor, this.isStale(generation));`.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A since-less read whose backward walk was ended by the page bound now returns the belonging messages it found and a `@parley-stream:<tail token>` (or last-message event_id) cursor, where today it returns `[]` and `@parley-stream:`.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Nothing — no input that is answered today becomes an error. Note the honest trade: the fix converts 'replay the whole room on the next start' into 'history deeper than MAX_BACKFILL_PAGES*limit is not reached by this window and its cursor sits at the tail', which is the same skip a since-less window already accepts for anything older than the window.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: None found. summary: The subscribe loop's retry ladder sleeps on the bare `delay()` from net-util, which is a plain unrefed-nothing `setTimeout` with no cancellation. `disconnect()` aborts every registered AbortController but cannot reach this sleep, so a Node timer of up to SYNC_RETRY_MAX_MS (30s) stays armed per subscribed topic after teardown, pinning the event loop. The package already owns the correct primitive twice over: `MatrixSession.interruptibleDelay` (used by `roomForRead`, registered in `this.controllers` so `standDown()` wakes it instantly) and net-util's `sleepUnlessStopped`, whose docstring names this exact hazard ('would otherwise stall disconnect() for 25 seconds and pin the event loop').
failure: Fake Synapse with `syncFailures = Infinity`. `connect()`, `subscribe('lifecycle')`, wait for 5 sync attempts (ladder at 200*2^4), then `disconnect()`. `disconnect()` resolves in 0ms, but instrumenting `globalThis.setTimeout`/`clearTimeout` and removing entries when the callback actually fires shows exactly one unfired timer left: `[3200]` ms. In steady state the ladder saturates at 30000ms, so a bridge whose homeserver is down keeps the process alive for up to 30s per topic past shutdown. `cli.ts` masks it with `process.exit(0)`; an embedder that awaits `bridge.shutdown()` and lets Node drain does not.
remediation: Change `MatrixSession.interruptibleDelay` from `private` to `protected` and replace `await delay(syncRetryDelayMs(consecutiveFailures));` in `subscribe`'s catch with `await this.interruptibleDelay(syncRetryDelayMs(consecutiveFailures));`. The `import { delay }` in index.ts stays live because `SYNC_IDLE_PACE_MS` still uses it, so the package's own dead-import scan is unaffected. Alternatively `sleepUnlessStopped(ms, () => this.isStale(generation))` from net-util, but that polls every 25ms rather than waking at the abort.

summary: `adoptRoom` JOINs before it reads provenance (correctly — a non-member cannot read room state), then throws if the creator or join rule fails the bar. The refusal therefore leaves the bridge account permanently joined to a room a stranger provisioned, and the plugin has no leave path. The README's security section describes the refusal as 'a room somebody else provisioned never receives this session's output and never feeds the agent its own' and never mentions the join it already made. Separately, because `ensureRoom` deletes the cache key on failure, every subsequent `post`/`fetchRecent` on a squatted topic re-issues `POST /join` + `GET /state` before throwing again — an unbounded re-probe of the attacker's room against the account's rate-limit budget.

The bridge's first `fetchRecent` on that topic issues `POST /rooms/<id>/join` (200), then `GET /state`, then throws the refusal. The account is now a member of the attacker's room forever; the README says nothing about it, and each retry repeats the join+state pair.

(1) Add a sentence to the README's 'Security — topic rooms are invite-only by default' section stating that the trust check happens after the join, so a refused room leaves this account joined and an operator must leave it out of band — the same treatment the read-path paragraph already gives ordinary joins. summary: `parley-xmpp`'s `parseArgs` silently ignores anything it does not recognise and falls back to `parley.config.yaml`. A mistyped flag, an unknown flag, `--help`, or a `--config` whose value the shell ate all start the bridge against a DIFFERENT deployment's config — its own `service`, `muc_service`, `identity.handle` and `topics` allowlist. Sibling packages already treat this as blocking: `bridge-redis` and `bridge-postgres` ship a hardened `src/args.ts` with an `error` arm that exits 2 plus a `cli-args.test.ts` that grades both the parser and the built binary; `bridge-xmpp` has neither, and no test in this package touches `cli.ts` at all.
failure: `parley-xmpp --confg /etc/parley/prod.yaml` -> `parseArgs` matches neither `--config`/`-c` nor the `--config=` prefix, so `config` stays `'parley.config.yaml'`; `loadConfig` reads the quickstart file in cwd and the bridge comes up posting agent output into the topics THAT config allowlists, with only a stderr line (routinely discarded by an MCP stdio host) to say so. Same for `parley-xmpp -c` as the final argv element (`next === undefined`, silently the default) and for `parley-xmpp --help` (runs a bridge instead of printing usage).
remediation: Extract the parse into `src/args.ts` returning a discriminated `{kind:'config'|'print'|'error'}` and have `cli.ts` exit 2 with USAGE on `error` and 0 on `print`, mirroring `packages/bridge-redis/src/args.ts` — the parser must refuse an argv it cannot honour rather than defaulting. Do not silently accept unknown flags.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "an argv the entrypoint cannot honour must stop it, not silently select another deployment." Port `bridge-redis/test/cli-args.test.ts` to this package: generate the rows from the flags USAGE declares (so a flag added later is graded before it has a bug), take the entrypoints from `package.json`'s `bin` (so a second bin is graded the day it lands), and run every row BOTH through the parser and through the built binary — a parser that refuses correctly guards nothing if `cli.ts` does not consult it. Include rows for: unknown flag, known flag with a missing value, `--config=` with an empty value, `--help`, `--version`, and a bare positional.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `packages/bridge-redis/src/args.ts` + `packages/bridge-redis/src/cli.ts` as the shipped shape (`args.kind === 'print'` -> stdout + exit 0; `args.kind === 'error'` -> stderr + USAGE + exit 2), and `packages/bridge-redis/test/cli-args.test.ts`'s staleness check (`newestSourceMtime`) so a spawned-binary row cannot pass against a stale `dist/`.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: `--help` and `--version`, which today are ignored and start a bridge.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `parley-xmpp --confg x.yaml`, `parley-xmpp -c` (no value), and any bare positional — today all silently accepted and answered with the default config.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I grepped every test file in `packages/bridge-xmpp/test/` for a reference to `src/cli.ts` or the `parley-xmpp` bin and found none, and `typecheck-coverage.test.ts` only asserts that `cli.ts` is inside a tsconfig project, not anything about its behaviour. I did NOT run a suite with the change applied, because the change is a new module.

If applied while the parse stays inline, the exit codes change but the duplication across ~12 packages remains — three of which have the hardened version and nine of which do not, which is the shape that let this one drift. summary: CI's guard against false green (`Assert no test file skipped entirely`, ci.yml) fails only when EVERY assertion in a file is skipped. `live-field-provenance.test.ts` has two unconditional describes plus `describe.skipIf(!secondAccount)`, so if `parley2@parley.local` cannot authenticate the ONLY case that grades co-occupant provenance against a real MUC silently vanishes and the file still reports pass. Nothing else in the repo gates on `SECOND_ACCOUNT`, so no other file's skip can surface it either — and `dev-infra.sh` reports a failed `prosodyctl register parley2` as "already present" (`|| log`), so the account not existing is not visible upstream either.
failure: Delete/expire the `parley2` account (or set `PARLEY_XMPP_PASS2` wrong) and run CI: `canAuth(SECOND_ACCOUNT)` returns false, `XMPP live provenance against a real MUC > a co-occupant cannot move timestamp or cursor with any child it can write` is skipped, the file's other 2 describes pass, the skip gate sees a file with non-skipped assertions and stays green — and the only real-server check that Prosody actually strips a forged `<stanza-id by='room'>`/`<delay from='room'>` (which I verified by hand that it does) is gone. I confirmed that case is load-bearing: it is one of the failures for mutations M1 and M2.
remediation: Make the requirement assertable rather than silently skippable: when `serverUp` is true but `secondAccount` is false, register a FAILING case naming the missing account (the server is up, so a second account is a provisioning bug, not an absent environment). Alternatively tighten CI's gate from "every file skipped entirely" to "no skipped assertion at all", which also closes it for `mam-paging.test.ts`.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a conditionally-gated describe whose condition can never be observed to have fired." Add a suite-shape test in this package that walks `test/**/*.test.ts`, collects every `describe.skipIf(...)`/`it.skipIf(...)` gate, and asserts each gating symbol is either (a) the whole file's only describe — so CI's file-level gate can see it — or (b) accompanied by a negative-control case that FAILS when the gate is off while the base server is up. Parameterize over the gate symbols found, not over a hand-list, so a new gate is graded the day it lands.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `live-xmpp.ts`'s `canAuth` returning a boolean rather than throwing, and `serverUp`/`secondAccount` already being computed as separate top-level awaits at lines 174-175 — so the "server up but second account missing" state is already distinguishable without new plumbing.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: a CI run where Prosody is up but `parley2` is not provisioned — today green, would go red.
