It would newly fail any environment (including a maintainer laptop) that runs the suite against a server with only the `parley` account; that is the intent, but it is a real behaviour change for local runs and should land with the dev-infra.sh registration made non-swallowing.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: It fixes the visibility of this one gate. If applied while `dev-infra.sh`'s `|| log "already present"` still masks a failed `prosodyctl register`, the failure is at least now loud in the test run rather than silent — but the provisioning script still lies about why.

summary: `"license": "MIT"` is declared but there is no `LICENSE` file in `packages/bridge-xmpp/` and `"files": ["dist"]`, so the published tarball carries a licence claim with no licence text. It is a recorded debt — `@sharptrick/parley-xmpp` is pinned in `packages/bridge-core/src/packaging.test.ts`'s `LICENSE_GAPS` — but the registry lives in another package and the fix lives here, so it will not close on its own.
failure: `npm pack` on this package produces a tarball whose only content is `dist/` plus the generated `package.json`/`README.md`; a consumer running `npx license-checker` (or any SBOM/attribution tool that reads licence TEXT rather than the SPDX field) gets `MIT` with no text to attribute. `find packages/bridge-xmpp -maxdepth 1` shows README.md, package.json, src, test, tsconfig*.json — no LICENSE.
remediation: Add `packages/bridge-xmpp/LICENSE` (a copy of the repo root MIT text) and remove `'@sharptrick/parley-xmpp'` from `LICENSE_GAPS` in `packages/bridge-core/src/packaging.test.ts` — that list is pinned EXACTLY, so leaving the entry after adding the file turns it into an unexpected-entry failure.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS rather than the entry: replace the `LICENSE_GAPS` allowlist with a per-workspace assertion that any package declaring a `license` field ships licence text npm will pack (a `LICENSE*` file in the package dir, which npm includes regardless of `files`), and keep a positive control proving the check can see a violation. An allowlist keyed by package name records the debt but cannot notice when a package is renamed or split.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: npm's rule that `LICENSE`/`LICENCE` files are always packed regardless of `files` — so no `package.json` change is needed; and `LICENSE_GAPS` being asserted exactly (the comment at packaging.test.ts:95 says closing one 'forces its removal here').
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none at runtime.

summary: `post` accepts a carriage return in `content` and stores an LF — the payload is silently altered rather than refused. The shared conformance suite's own words are that "refusing a payload is a visible, legitimate answer; altering it silently is not", and `packages/conformance/src/cases/post.ts:9-16` explicitly withholds the CR fidelity row BECAUSE bridge-xmpp accepts it. That is the shared suite's coverage being narrowed to fit one backend, which is the shape the prime directive exists to surface.
failure: `post(t, h, 'a\rb')` resolves; `fetchRecent(t)` returns `content === 'a\nb'`. Core stores the returned `backendMsgId` for a message whose bytes it never sent, and an agent that round-trips a CRLF document through Parley gets a different document back with no error. `assertXmlSafe` deliberately permits #x9/#xA/#xD (stanzas.ts:64), which is correct for XML validity but is also what lets the CR reach the wire and be normalized.
remediation: Either refuse a CR in `post` content with an error naming the codepoint and the reason (matching the treatment of every other codepoint the stream cannot carry), and then add the `['a carriage return', 'fidelity\rsecond line']` row to `postCases`; or, if refusing is judged worse than normalizing, keep the behaviour and record the adjudication in the commit message rather than in the README paragraph, which currently reads as prose aimed at a reviewer (CLAUDE.md: 'never as a comment, a doc paragraph, or defensive prose aimed at the next reviewer').
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "the seam silently rewrites caller content" rather than the CR instance: widen `postCases`' fidelity table into a generator over every codepoint the transport is known to transform (XML line-ending normalization #xD and #xD#xA; and, per backend, any protocol-level trimming), asserting the plugin either round-trips it byte-for-byte or REJECTS it with a non-empty message — never a third answer. Then no backend can be accommodated by deleting a row.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `wire.assertXmlSafe(content, 'post content')` at index.ts:151, which is already the single choke point every `post` passes through, and `xmlIllegalCodepoint`'s `if (cp === 0x9 || cp === 0xa || cp === 0xd) continue;` — the CR arm would have to move out of that skip into a separate content-only check, NOT into `assertXmlSafe` itself, which also screens config values and the RSM cursor where a CR is not the same hazard.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `post(t, h, 'line1\r\nline2')` — any CRLF-terminated text an agent pastes from a Windows source. This is a real usability cost and is the reason the current behaviour may have been chosen deliberately.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: I did not apply this change, so I did not measure it. By inspection, `packages/bridge-xmpp/test/content-fidelity.test.ts` and `packages/bridge-xmpp/test/xml-hostile-content.test.ts` both carry CR-related rows and would need updating; the shared `postCases` table has no CR row today so it would not break.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If the refusal is added and the conformance row is NOT added, the class stays open — the suite still cannot see a backend that silently rewrites content. If neither is done, the defect is that the shared suite's coverage is set by this plugin's limitation and nothing records that as debt.

summary: `assertKnownConfigKeys` polices only TOP-LEVEL backend_config keys. `tls` is passed to `connectionOptions` unvalidated in both key-set and type, so a typo inside it is silently dropped — the exact failure the function's own JSDoc says it exists to refuse ('A key this plugin does not read is a key it silently drops').
failure: `backend_config: { tls: { ca_flie: '/etc/parley/ca.pem' } }` (or `cert_flie`/`keyfile`) → `connect()` succeeds, no warning, and `connectionOptions` returns `opts.tls = { caFile: undefined, certFile: undefined, keyFile: undefined }` (reproduced). TLS is still required by nats.js, but the pinned CA is gone and the link verifies against the system trust store instead — and with `cert_file`/`key_file` misspelled the client presents NO certificate, so against a server that offers but does not require mTLS the connection succeeds and the operator believes mutual TLS is in force. `plaintextCredentialRisks` also suppresses its warning for any non-undefined `tls`, so `tls: true` / `tls: "yes"` silence the plaintext-credential warning while supplying no material at all.
remediation: Extend the key check one level: after `assertKnownConfigKeys`, if `cfg.tls !== undefined` require it to be a plain object and reject any key outside `ca_file|cert_file|key_file`, and reject a non-string value for each. Reuse the same message shape ('unknown backend_config key tls.<k> — expected one of ...').
testUpgrade: Class: 'a config value the plugin reads STRUCTURALLY is validated only at its outermost level'. Replace the flat near-miss generator in config.test.ts ('generates a near miss for every declared key') with one that walks the declared shape recursively — derive leaf paths from the exported `NatsBackendConfig` source (helpers.ts already parses that interface) including nested members, and assert every near-miss of every PATH is refused at connect() naming the path. Parameterize over `{ typo-at-leaf, wrong-scalar-type-at-leaf, wrong-container-type }` so the same table also covers `tls: true` and any future nested field. Existing too-narrow test: config.test.ts:411 `refuses backend_config.${typo}` — its `declaredConfigKeys()` regex `^ {2}([a-z_]+)\??:` matches two-space-indented members only, so `tls`'s children are invisible to it by construction.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `assertKnownConfigKeys(config)` in session.ts:39, which already runs before `connectionOptions`, and `connectionOptions`'s branch `if (cfg.tls !== undefined) { opts.tls = { caFile: cfg.tls.ca_file, ... } }` (config.ts:237) which the fix leaves untouched.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `backend_config: { tls: { ca_flie: '/x' } }` and `backend_config: { tls: true }` — both accepted today.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I grepped every `tls:` literal in packages/bridge-nats/test and examples/multi-session/nats: config.test.ts:88/434/586/702 all pass `{ ca_file, cert_file, key_file }` subsets, and transport-agreement-live.test.ts:56 passes `tls: {}`. The EMPTY object must keep passing — a fix that requires at least one known sub-key breaks that live test, so the rule must be 'no UNKNOWN sub-key', not 'at least one known sub-key'.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied, nothing about the drop stays broken — the typo becomes a load error. What it does NOT fix is `plaintextCredentialRisks` treating any `tls` value as proof of encryption; that stays correct only because nats.js genuinely fails fast when `opts.tls` is set and the server offers none (pinned by transport-agreement-live.test.ts:53).

summary: `validateRetentionDays` rejects `0` because 'JetStream reads max_age: 0 as UNLIMITED, so retention_days: 0 would mean the exact opposite of what an operator wrote' — but it validates the DAYS while `streams.ts` does the nanosecond conversion, so a positive value that rounds to zero nanoseconds slips through and produces the very `max_age: 0` the guard names.
failure: `backend_config: { retention_days: 1e-15 }` → `validateRetentionDays` returns 1e-15 (finite, positive), `ensureStream` computes `Math.round(1e-15 * 86_400_000_000_000) === 0` and calls `streams.add({ name, subjects, max_age: 0 })`. Reproduced: `fake.state.added === { name: 'PARLEY_deploys', subjects: ['parley.deploys'], max_age: 0 }`. The stream is created with UNLIMITED retention and, because `max_age` is locked in at creation, permanently — the exact inversion the validator documents itself as preventing, and unrecoverable without out-of-band `nats stream edit`.
remediation: Validate the composed value rather than the input: move `NS_PER_DAY` and the `Math.round` into `validateRetentionDays`, have it return the nanosecond `max_age`, and reject when that rounds below 1 with a message naming the composed nanoseconds — the same 'judge the prefix by the name it composes' pattern `validatePrefix` already uses. `ensureStream` then assigns `config.max_age = this.retentionMaxAgeNs` with no arithmetic of its own.
testUpgrade: Class: 'a value validated in the operator's unit, applied in the backend's unit, where the conversion can re-enter the rejected region'. Widen the `retentions` table in config.test.ts:118 from a hand-enumerated list to a generator over the CONVERSION's boundary — `{1e-15, 1e-12, 5e-15, 1/NS_PER_DAY, 0.5/NS_PER_DAY, 2/NS_PER_DAY}` plus the existing rows — and assert the invariant, not the row: for every accepted value, `state.added.max_age >= 1`; for every rejected value, `addCalls === 0`. That form also catches a future unit change (ms→ns) and any other field that composes through a rounding step. Existing too-narrow test: config.test.ts:144, whose smallest positive row is `0.5`, twelve orders of magnitude above the boundary.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `streams.ts:69` `config.max_age = Math.round(this.retentionDays * NS_PER_DAY)` — the only reader of `retentionDays`, and `session.ts:43` `const retentionDays = validateRetentionDays(cfg.retention_days)`, the only caller. `NS_PER_DAY` is currently declared in streams.ts:10 and must move or be duplicated.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `retention_days: 1e-15` (and anything below ~5.8e-15 days), accepted today.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: config.test.ts:144's rows are `{undefined, 30, 1, 0.5}` accepted and `{0,-0,-1,-0.5,NaN,±Infinity,'30','thirty',null,true,[]}` rejected — all keep their verdict under the fix, and `0.5 * NS_PER_DAY = 4.32e13 >= 1`. The row asserts `state.added.max_age` directly, so if the fix changes what `retentionDays` HOLDS (days→ns) the production code must change with it or that assertion goes red; the assertion itself does not need editing.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Applied, the whole class closes because the check now sits on the value actually sent. If instead one only tightened the days-side bound (e.g. `days < 1e-9` rejected), the guard would still be validating the wrong quantity and any future change to NS_PER_DAY or to the rounding would re-open it.

summary: `delay(ms)` never clears its `setTimeout`, and it is used as the losing side of four `Promise.race`s (`disconnect()`'s closer race and drain race, `EphemeralConsumer.reap()`, `blockingFetch`'s closer). `Promise.race` does not cancel the loser, so every one of those leaves a live 2000ms timer that keeps the Node event loop alive after the operation it bounded has finished.
failure: Reproduced against a real server with the built `dist/`: connect → post → 3× fetchRecent → `await disconnect()`. `disconnect()` returns at 532ms; the process does not exit until 2530ms — a full `DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS` after teardown completed, with nothing left to do. Each `pull()` also leaves one such timer per read via its `finally { await ephemeral.reap() }`, so a bridge doing catch-up polls carries a rolling pool of pending 2s timers proportional to its read rate. The CLI masks this with `process.exit(0)`; anything embedding the plugin (the conformance harness, any host process that awaits `disconnect()` and expects to exit) pays the 2s.
remediation: Add a cancelling race helper next to `delay` — `const raceWithin = async <T>(p: Promise<T>, ms: number) => { let t; try { return await Promise.race([p, new Promise<void>(r => { t = setTimeout(r, ms); })]); } finally { clearTimeout(t); } }` — and use it at session.ts:96, session.ts:104, jetstream.ts:70 and pull.ts:122. Leave bare `delay` for the sites that AWAIT it to completion (read.ts:49 absent-stream poll, live.ts:48 backoff). Do not reach for `.unref()`: at those two await sites an unref'd timer lets the process exit mid-poll if nothing else holds the loop.
testUpgrade: Class: 'a bounded wait implemented as a race leaves its loser running'. Add a parameterized case over every teardown path already tabled in resource-live.test.ts:342 (`${life.name} leaves no socket and no consumer once disconnected`) that additionally asserts the event loop is released — spawn a child `node` that connects, exercises the path, awaits `disconnect()`, and assert the child's exit happens within a small multiple of the time `disconnect()` itself took, rather than within `DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS`. Parameterizing over the existing `life` rows means a new teardown path that reintroduces an uncancelled race fails by default. Nothing today grades event-loop release at all.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `session.ts:96` `await Promise.race([Promise.all(closing), delay(DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS)])`, `session.ts:104` `await Promise.race([nc.drain().catch(...), delay(DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS)])`, `jetstream.ts:70` `await Promise.race([this.adding, delay(DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS)])`, `pull.ts:122` `await Promise.race([cleanup, delay(DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS)])`. All four keep the same settle semantics — only the loser's timer is cleared.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — no input-space change; this is purely a resource-release change.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I looked at outage.test.ts's `disconnect() with ${teardown.name} returns within its budget` rows (they assert an UPPER bound on `disconnect()`'s own duration, which the fix cannot raise) and resource-live.test.ts:342/379, which assert server-side consumer and socket counts after disconnect, unaffected by whether a client timer is cleared. I did not run the suite with the fix applied.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while some other path still leaks a timer, the process still lingers — the fix is per-site, so the testUpgrade above (which measures the OBSERVABLE, process exit) matters more than the edit. Nothing about correctness or teardown ordering is hidden either way: today's behaviour is a delay, never a wrong answer.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The settle semantics are unchanged at all four sites: the helper still resolves on whichever of {work, timeout} lands first, and `clearTimeout` runs in a `finally` after that decision, so a timeout that fires in the same tick as completion is still honoured or still discarded exactly as today. Two callers on the new path do not share state — each invocation closes over its own `t` — so `disconnect()` racing an in-flight `pull()`'s `reap()` behaves as it does now: `disconnect()` splices and runs closers, `pull`'s `finally` finds `indexOf === -1` and no-ops, and each of the two `raceWithin` calls clears only its own timer.

summary: Nothing in the suite grades the size of `this.subscriptions`. `NatsSession.unregister()` — the only thing that bounds the read path's teardown registry — can be replaced with a complete no-op and all 1711 tests stay green, including the whole live resource-hygiene file.
failure: Mutation applied and isolated (jetstream.ts and pull.ts restored to original first): `protected unregister(closer: Closeable): void { void closer; }` → `24 test files passed, 1711 tests passed`. With that mutation live, every `fetchRecent` and every `blockingFetch` permanently appends a `Closeable` to an array only `disconnect()` ever drains, so a long-running bridge — whose whole job is core polling `fetchRecent` — grows the array without bound, and `disconnect()` then fires N `ephemeral.reap()` calls (N uncancelled 2s timers, see the previous finding). `resource-live.test.ts` counts consumers ON THE SERVER, which the mutation does not change, and no test reads the client-side array at all.
remediation: This is a coverage hole, not a live defect — `pull` and `blockingFetch` do unregister in their `finally` today. The remedy belongs in the suite, not the source.
testUpgrade: Class: 'a client-side teardown registry whose growth is invisible to every server-side leak assertion'. In resource.test.ts (fake-backed, ungated), add a parameterized case over the read shapes already tabled there (`fetchRecent`, `fetchRecent` with `since`, `blockMs` long-poll, a read whose stream vanishes mid-flight, a read that throws in `get`/`fetch`/`iterate`) that snapshots `(plugin as unknown as { subscriptions: unknown[] }).subscriptions.length` before and after N=20 iterations and demands it be UNCHANGED — reached through the same private-field cast the file already uses, and asserting the invariant (bounded) rather than a literal count, so a refactor that moves the registry elsewhere reddens rather than silently passing. Crossing it with the fault rows matters: the shape that would actually regress is a read that throws before its `finally`.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `pull.ts:46` `this.subscriptions.push(closer)` / `pull.ts:81` `this.unregister(closer)`, `pull.ts:126`/`pull.ts:157` for `blockingFetch`, and `session.ts:87` `this.subscriptions.splice(0)`. Note `subscribe()` (live.ts:36) pushes a closer it never unregisters — that is bounded by the number of subscribed topics, so the new assertion must be scoped to read shapes or take subscribe's contribution as its baseline.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — no production change.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none — this is additive. I confirmed the new assertion has a defect to catch by watching the no-op mutation stay green across the full suite.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is broken today, so applying this changes no behaviour; what it buys is that the next edit to a read path's `finally` cannot silently unbound the registry. If the testUpgrade were written against a literal count instead of 'unchanged from baseline', it would cement the current registration layout — the thing CLAUDE.md's architectural-test rule warns about.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The new assertion must not run concurrently with an in-flight read: `subscriptions` is mutated by `pull`'s push and its `finally` unregister, so a snapshot taken while a read is pending legitimately reads one higher. Take both snapshots between fully-awaited calls, and if the case is ever extended to concurrent reads, assert the post-settle length rather than any mid-flight value.

summary: `parseArgs` silently ignores a `--config`/`-c` with no following value and silently ignores every unrecognised argument, so a mistyped invocation loads the DEFAULT config path instead of failing. The file is the package's published `bin` entry point and has zero tests in this package.
failure: `parley-nats --config` (value omitted) → `next === undefined`, `config` stays `process.env.PARLEY_CONFIG ?? 'parley.config.yaml'`, and the bridge comes up on whatever that path holds — a different cluster, a different topic allowlist, a different identity — printing `parley-nats: bridge up` as if the operator's request had been honoured. summary: The plugin is a five-deep chain of abstract classes — `NatsSession` → `NatsStreams` → `NatsPulls` → `NatsReads` → `NatsLive` → `NatsPlugin` — each with exactly one subclass and no other implementation. The chain is a file split wearing an inheritance costume: it buys no polymorphism, and every level reaches into the same mutable `protected` state (`subscriptions`, `incarnations`, `ensured`, `stopped`, `epoch`, `subjectPrefix`).
failure: Not a runtime failure; an observable structural cost. Because no level is independently instantiable, every test that needs one reaches through the concrete leaf with a cast — `injectFake` writes `peek.js`/`peek.jsm`/`peek.ensured`/`peek.incarnations` through `plugin as unknown as {...}` (fake-jetstream.ts:411), docs.test.ts casts twice to reach `subject`/`streamName`/`msgId`/`cursorAt`, lifecycle/recovery/names/prefix-live each cast once. The seam's own contract (`connect/disconnect/subscribe/post/fetchRecent/resolveIdentity`) is six methods; nothing about it asks for five inheritance levels, and a reader tracing `this.stopped` has to know which of six files owns it.
remediation: Replace the chain with composition: keep `NatsSession` as a concrete owner of the link, the epoch and the closer registry, and have `NatsPlugin` hold one — `private readonly session: NatsSession` — passing it to free functions or small collaborators for streams/pulls/reads/live. The shared state then has one owner with an explicit interface, and the fake can be injected through that seam instead of through a cast at a private field.
testUpgrade: Class: 'a structure asserted by reaching through a private member of a concrete leaf'. Give `injectFake` a supported injection point — e.g. an exported test seam on the session object, or a constructor parameter for the JetStream handles — and rewrite the casts against it. Then add ONE architectural case, written as a glob over `src/**` rather than a file list, asserting the invariant rather than the layout: no exported class in this package has more than one `extends` ancestor within the package. Per CLAUDE.md, if that ratchet is what stands between the code and a better shape, the ratchet is what is wrong — so state it as a bound on depth, not as the current six names.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: Every `protected` member of session.ts (`subjectPrefix`, `streamPrefix`, `retentionDays`, `stopped`, `epoch`, `ensured`, `incarnations`, `subscriptions`, `live()`, `unregister`, `requireJs`, `requireJsm`) and every call site of them across streams.ts, pull.ts, read.ts, live.ts, index.ts.

remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: fake-jetstream.ts's `injectFake` and `attachConnection` (they write `plugin.js`, `plugin.jsm`, `plugin.nc`, `plugin.ensured`, `plugin.incarnations` directly), and therefore, transitively, every fake-backed file: window, cursor, cursor-input, resource, msg-id, subscribe-loop, long-poll, payload, recovery, lifecycle, config. That is roughly 1400 of the 1711 tests depending on one cast in one helper — which is itself the strongest evidence for the finding, and the strongest argument for doing the injection-point half FIRST and the decomposition second.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is broken today; this is maintainability debt, and a botched refactor is strictly worse than the chain. I would land the injection seam alone and leave the chain until a second implementation actually needs it.
remediationCheck.interleavings: n/a — the refactor moves state ownership without changing when it is read or written, but that is exactly what must be preserved: `epoch` is bumped by `disconnect()` before closers run and read by `subscribe`'s `running()`/`retired()` closures, so a composition that puts `epoch` behind an async accessor would reopen the teardown race the current synchronous field closes. Keep every epoch and `stopped` read synchronous.

summary: The transport-safety grid builds 8 schemes × 10 hosts × secret × tls = 320 `it.each` cells, each running a full `connect()`/`disconnect()` — but the scheme axis is separately and completely proven inert by the test three lines above it, and each lookalike host is separately proven remote by the `it.each(LOOKALIKE_HOSTS)` beside it. 280 of the 320 rows are near-copies that cannot fail independently of the 40 they duplicate.

summary: `budgetedDeadlineMs` turns the caller's remaining `blockMs` into the transport deadline for every history read the call makes, so a Zulip whose `GET /api/v1/messages` latency exceeds the residual budget makes `fetchRecent` REJECT instead of returning the empty page the seam requires at timeout. It reaches both `index.ts:108` (the mandatory first read) and `wake.ts:23` (every read inside the wait).

Expected in every case: `{messages: [], nextCursor: since}` (packages/conformance/src/cases/blocking.ts, clause `native-block-actually-waits`). Core does not absorb it: engine/blocking-fetch.ts awaits `plugin.fetchRecent(...)` directly, so the rejection is the whole `parley_fetch_recent` tool call.
remediation: Separate the two things `deadlineMs` currently conflates in `@sharptrick/parley-net-util`'s `fetchWithRetry`: the per-attempt abort budget and the ceiling on a 429 wait. Add an option (e.g. `maxRetryWaitMs`) so a caller can say "one attempt gets a normal request budget, but never sleep past X". Then, for reads made inside a `blockMs`, pass `deadlineMs: DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS` and `maxRetryWaitMs: <residual>` instead of `deadlineMs: residual + 500`. `pacing.budgetedDeadlineMs` then becomes the retry-wait ceiling, which is exactly what its own doc comment says it is for. Do NOT fix it by skipping the read when the budget is spent — see remediationCheck.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a mandatory request whose transport budget is derived from a caller's WAIT budget fails on latency the wait was never about. Parameterize `blocking-fetch.test.ts`'s SLOW_STATES over `holdResponse(route, ms)` for EVERY route the call touches — including `GET /api/v1/messages`, which today appears only as a 429 row — crossed with the existing `[200, 600, 2000]` budgets and with both wake sources (piggyback vs dedicated queue), asserting `{messages: [], nextCursor: since}` and never a rejection whenever the slow answer is mere latency rather than a server-stated wait. Widen the latency generator to straddle `REQUEST_ANSWER_MS` (e.g. 100/400/700/1500) so the boundary is generated rather than picked. Existing tests too narrow to catch this: `blocking-fetch.test.ts` SLOW_STATES (no plain-latency row on the history read), `long-poll-deadline.test.ts` (grades only PARKING requests), `units.test.ts` `"a request inside a caller's budget gets what is left of it, plus one answer"` (grades the formula, pinning `budgetedDeadlineMs(spent) === 500` as if 500ms were always enough).

The fix depends on splitting exactly those two uses; nothing in packages/bridge-zulip can express it alone.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: `fetchRecent({topic, since: tail, blockMs: 100})` against a server with 700ms history-read latency: today it rejects at 606ms; after the fix it returns a page (possibly empty) at ~700ms — i.e. it overruns `blockMs` by up to one request latency.

The `rejects: true` row (429 on the history read) keeps passing, because `maxRetryWaitMs` still refuses an 8s hint inside a 600ms budget. Applying the naive alternative instead (skip the read once the budget is spent) HIDES the symptom on two of the four repros while silently dropping a message the caller could have had.

summary: On the blocking path the REST pager is given `deadlineMs = budgetMs` (the long-poll's remaining time), so net-util refuses any 429 whose stated wait exceeds it — instantly, long before the deadline — and `fetchWithin`'s swallow (`Date.now() >= walk.deadline`) is false at that moment, so the whole `fetch_recent` rejects. Core's `fetchRecentBlocking` does not catch a plugin rejection and `tools.ts` rethrows anything that is not abort/NoSuchTopic, so ONE routine Discord rate limit ends the entire long-poll as an `isError` tool result. It gets worse as the budget drains: core re-issues each iteration with `blockMs: remaining`, so at 59.5s into a 60s budget a 429 asking for 600ms is fatal.
failure: Reproduced against unmutated source by instrumenting `settle()` in blocking-budget.test.ts: `plugin.fetchRecent({topic, since: '1', blockMs: 1500})` against a channel answering `429 {retry_after: 20}` rejects with `HttpStatusError: Discord GET /channels/780002176/messages?after=1&limit=100 → 429: upstream asked for 20000ms, past this call's 1489ms deadline (5ms elapsed)`. The identical 429 on a non-blocking `fetchRecent` is waited out inside the 30000ms default and succeeds. Expected per seam.ts and the plugin's own JSDoc: `{ messages: [], nextCursor: since }` — replayable, with core polling the rest of its budget.
remediation: In `fetchWithin`, widen the swallow from 'the clock is already past the deadline' to also cover a retryable rate limit: `if (statusOf(err) === 429) { warn(...); return { messages: [], nextCursor: walk.since }; }` before the existing deadline check (`statusOf` is exported from @sharptrick/parley-net-util). The same shape reaches the non-blocking walk via `pageWithin` for `limit > 100`, so the equivalent treatment belongs on a later page there too: a 429 that cannot be waited out inside the remaining budget should end the walk with what it gathered, not fail the call.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a retryable provider refusal inside a bounded call becomes a tool error instead of an empty replayable page'. Parameterize over (entry point: blocking fetchRecent / catch-up fetchRecent with limit>100 / since-less fetchRecent) x (refusal: 429 with a hint above the remaining budget, 429 with a hint below it, a stalled response, a transport reset) x (budget: 1, 250, 1500, 60000 ms) and assert the OUTCOME, not just the latency: resolves with `messages: []` and `nextCursor === since` (or the last message kept), never rejects. The existing `blocking-budget.test.ts` cells are exactly this table but assert only elapsed time, which is why they are green today.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: net-util `statusOf` (errors.ts, re-exported from index.ts) and `HttpStatusError`, which fetchWithRetry throws for the over-deadline 429 branch: `throw new HttpStatusError(opts.label, 429, stated && overDeadline ? ... )`. Also relies on core's `fetchRecentBlocking` advancing `since = result.nextCursor` on an empty page, which for `nextCursor === since` is a no-op, so the next poll iteration re-queries the same window.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A blocking `fetchRecent` whose page query is refused with 429 now resolves `{messages: [], nextCursor: since}` where it rejects today.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I checked: rest-contract.test.ts '429 rate limits' drives `post` (not on the fetchWithin path); readme.test.ts 'refuses a stated wait past the call deadline' drives `post`; disconnect-quiescence.test.ts's '429 backoff: fetchRecent (blockMs)' maps both settlements to a string it never asserts; blocking-budget.test.ts uses the same outcome-erasing `settle()`. That absence of a red test is itself the second finding.

That is the seam-correct answer (core polls and the cursor is replayable) but it does trade a loud failure for a quiet one, which is why the warn() line is part of the fix rather than optional.

summary: `const settle = (call) => call.then(() => 'resolved', () => 'rejected')` maps both settlements to a string that no cell ever asserts; every one of the 14 cells then checks only `Date.now() - started <= BLOCK_MS + SLACK_MS`. A call that THROWS satisfies that bound trivially. The suite is named 'a blocking fetchRecent settles inside blockMs when it stalls on ...' but grades latency only, so the seam behaviour it exists to protect — an empty page with a replayable cursor — is ungraded.
failure: Mutation MUT-AH: replace the whole body of `DiscordPlugin.fetchWithin` (index.ts:161-169) with `return await this.fetchSince(walk);`, deleting the deadline swallow and the NoSuchTopicError passthrough. Where a rejection is the intended answer, name it per-cell with the error text expected rather than swallowing it in a shared helper.

summary: `pageRecords` (wire.ts:110) exists to REFUSE a whole page containing an unusable record — its comment says a filter 'cannot advance the cursor past the record it dropped — core resumes strictly after it and can never come back'. But `expectSeamSafe`, and the comment above it ('the table still holds if the refusal ever becomes a filter'), deliberately accept the filter arm. The one property the function was written to protect is therefore the one property the table does not grade.
failure: Mutation MUT-K: change `pageRecords` to `return body.filter(hasUsableId) as DiscordMessage[]`. Full suite: 881/881 PASS. The cell 'fetchRecent (since) on a page whose OLDER record has an empty-string id' then returns one message ('newer', cursor 300000000000000002) and drops the older record permanently — core persists 300000000000000002 as `since` and queries `?after=` it forever. `expectSeamSafe` passes: every returned message has a usable key, `nextCursor === messages.at(-1).cursor`, and `BigInt(nextCursor) >= BigInt(since)`. Silent, unrecoverable message loss with the whole suite green.
remediation: Add the missing invariant to `expectSeamSafe`: on a page that contained an unusable record, the call must either reject OR return every usable record on that page — i.e. `messages.length` must equal the number of usable records in the injected body, never fewer. Then the 'OLDER record has ...' rows fail under a filter, because the filter returns 1 of 2 while the refusal returns 0 and rejects.

summary: `this.seq` (the last dispatch sequence, echoed in every heartbeat) is reset to null only in `restart()`, i.e. on `connect()`. Nothing resets it on a RECONNECT: `stopSocket()`, `scheduleReconnect()`, `dial()` and `openSocket()` all leave it. Discord's heartbeat `d` is the last sequence received ON THIS CONNECTION (null when none), and this plugin deliberately never RESUMEs, so every reconnected socket's pre-READY heartbeats advertise a sequence belonging to a session that no longer exists.
failure: Socket S1 reaches READY and receives dispatches up to s=57, then closes 1006. The ladder dials S2 and re-IDENTIFYs (fresh session, no RESUME). If a heartbeat fires before S2's READY, the plugin sends `{op:1, d:57}` on a connection that has received nothing. Contract says `d: null`. Additionally, mutation MUT-AD (delete `this.seq = null` from `restart()`) leaves 881/881 green, so even the connect()-time reset that DOES exist is untested — `wire-contract.test.ts`'s 'before READY, with nothing dispatched yet → seq null' only ever runs against a virgin plugin.
remediation: Reset `this.seq = null` at the start of `openSocket` (per connection) rather than only in `restart` (per session), so the value is scoped to the socket that produced it — the same scoping `heartbeats` and `awaitedAck` already have.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'per-connection gateway state scoped to the session instead of the socket'. Parameterize `wire-contract.test.ts`'s heartbeat-seq PHASES over the socket's generation (first socket / after a transient close+reconnect / after connect()+connect()), asserting `heartbeatSeqs().at(-1)` equals what THAT socket dispatched — `FakeWs.seqSent()` already returns exactly that, so the assertion compares two per-socket values and cannot be satisfied by session-scoped state.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `openSocket` already runs the `isStopped()/epoch` guard before creating the socket, so a reset there cannot clobber a live socket's seq from a retired dial. `this.seq` is read only inside the heartbeat interval and the op-1 echo, both closed over `ws`.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — `wire-contract.test.ts`'s 'after a run of dispatches' expects seq 4 on the SAME socket that dispatched 2,3,4, which a per-socket reset preserves. 'on a socket the plugin has superseded' asserts silence, unaffected. I did not run this mutation in the fix direction.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Impact is low: with RESUME unused, Discord does not act on a stale heartbeat `d`. If the plugin ever adds RESUME, a stale seq becomes a real replay/gap bug — this closes it before that.

summary: The Rate limits table's third row states the failure threshold as 'a hint longer than the call's remaining budget (**30000 ms**)', and `readme.test.ts` pins `DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS` as `30000 ms` in that section. On the hot path the threshold is `block_ms` — shrinking toward zero as the budget drains — not 30000 ms. The section's operator advice ('Discord's global rate limits routinely ask for longer than 30000 ms ... reduce the load on the bot token') therefore understates by orders of magnitude how routine the failure is: a 429 asking for 2s already fails a `block_ms: 1500` call.

The test that is supposed to bind this prose to behaviour asserts only that the string `30000 ms` appears.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `readme.test.ts` already slices `## Rate limits` .. `## Provisioning` and already has a working driven-prose pattern in the gateway-failure describe block; the fake's `injectFault({status:429, body:{retry_after}})` supplies both hint sizes.

summary: `fetchRecent` accepts `blockMs` straight into deadline arithmetic with no finiteness check. `NaN` and `Infinity` are neither `> 0` nor `<= 0`, so every comparison in `SlackHistory.blockForMessage` answers false and the ladder loop never terminates. This is the exact class the plugin already defends for `limit` ("the seam declares `limit?: number` with no floor, and this is the only layer that can keep one", history.ts:47) and that core refuses explicitly in engine/blocking-fetch.ts:109 ("A non-finite budget is neither `> 0` nor `<= 0`, so every deadline comparison below answers false and the loop naps forever"). The plugin's own loop re-implements that loop without the guard.
failure: `plugin.fetchRecent({ topic, since: asCursor('0'), blockMs: NaN })` against the in-process fake never settles and issued 1084 `conversations.history` requests in 1.5 s (~720/s, sustained until disconnect) — against Slack's tiered-limit read method. `plugin.fetchRecent({ topic, since, blockMs: Infinity })` never settles either (3 reads, then parked forever). Reproduced in this worktree; both calls returned 'HUNG' against a 1.5 s race.
remediation: In `SlackPlugin.fetchRecent`, normalize the budget before it becomes a deadline, exactly as `runFetch` floors `limit`: `const asked = args.blockMs ?? 0; const blockMs = Number.isFinite(asked) ? asked : 0;` — a non-finite budget then falls into the existing `blockMs <= 0` immediate-return branch. Belt-and-braces, add `if (!Number.isFinite(remaining)) break;` next to the `if (remaining <= 0) break;` in `blockForMessage`, so a future caller that reaches the ladder directly cannot spin it.
testUpgrade: Widen catchup-window.test.ts's existing CLASS — 'a seam argument used in arithmetic without a floor' — from `limit` to EVERY numeric field of `FetchRecentArgs`, as one table: rows `{limit: [-5,-1,0,1,NaN,Infinity,-Infinity,undefined]} × {blockMs: [-1,0,NaN,Infinity,-Infinity,50]} × {since: [none, '0']}`, each asserting the call settles inside a fixed wall-clock bound AND that `fake.hits('conversations.history')` stays under a wall-clock-derived ceiling. The existing LIMIT_ROWS table cannot catch this: it never varies `blockMs` and never asserts settlement time.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `Number.isFinite`, and the existing branch in index.ts:152 `if (blockMs <= 0 || args.since === undefined || first.messages.length > 0) return first;` — the fix depends on the `blockMs <= 0` arm being the immediate-return path, which it is.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — `blockMs: NaN` and `blockMs: Infinity` already 'succeed' today in the sense that they are not rejected; after the fix they return the catch-up window at once instead of hanging.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none, if the clamp form is used (it degrades rather than throws, matching how `limit` is handled). If you instead copy core's `RangeError` form, it newly rejects `blockMs: NaN` / `Infinity`, which is a behaviour change on a public seam method and would need its own row.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I grepped every `blockMs:` site under packages/bridge-slack/test and packages/conformance/src: every one is a finite literal or a finite constant (BLOCK_MS, DEGRADED_BLOCK_MS, BACKLOG_BLOCK_MS, HANDSHAKE_MS/4), and core's `fetchRecentBlocking` always hands the plugin `Math.max(0, remaining)` after its own finiteness refusal. I did not run the full suite with the fix applied.

summary: `parseArgs` silently ignores every argument it does not recognise, and silently ignores `--config` when no value follows it, falling back to `$PARLEY_CONFIG` or `./parley.config.yaml`. For Slack that default names a different deployment: a different `bot_token`, `app_token` and `channel_map`, i.e. a different workspace and a different bot identity. `packages/bridge-redis/src/args.ts` and `packages/bridge-postgres/src/args.ts` already ship the corrected shape (a `{run|print|error}` union, `--help`/`--version`, `exit 2` with usage) with `test/cli-args.test.ts` behind it; bridge-slack kept the pre-fix inline parser and has no CLI test at all.
failure: `parley-slack --config` (the shell ate the path, or a wrapper interpolated an empty variable) → the missing-value branch is skipped, `config` stays `parley.config.yaml`, `loadConfig` succeeds, and the bridge comes up on stderr saying `bridge up — handle=… topics=[…]` against the WRONG workspace's tokens and channel map, exit code 0. Likewise `parley-slack --help` starts a bridge and blocks instead of printing usage, and `parley-slack -c a.yaml b.yaml` silently drops `b.yaml`.
remediation: Extract `packages/bridge-slack/src/args.ts` mirroring `packages/bridge-redis/src/args.ts` verbatim in shape: `USAGE`, a `SLACK_VERSION` read from package.json, `ParsedArgs = {kind:'run',config} | {kind:'print',text} | {kind:'error',message}`, `--help`/`-h`, `--version`/`-V`, an error when `--config`'s value is absent or starts with `-`, an error for `--config=` with an empty value, and an error for any unrecognised argument. `cli.ts` then branches on `kind` and `process.exit(2)` on error, as redis/postgres already do.
testUpgrade: Add `packages/bridge-slack/test/cli-args.test.ts` as a table over argv shapes shared in spirit with the redis/postgres one — `[]`, `['--config']`, `['-c']`, `['--config','-x']`, `['--config=']`, `['--config=a.yaml']`, `['a.yaml']`, `['--verbose']`, `['--help']`, `['--version']`, `['-c','a.yaml','b.yaml']` — each asserting the `kind` and, for `run`, the resolved config path, with `PARLEY_CONFIG` set and unset. Guard the CLASS by asserting that NO argv reaching `kind:'run'` came from an argument the parser did not consume, so a future flag added without a branch fails here rather than being ignored.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `packages/bridge-redis/src/args.ts` as the shipped reference implementation, including its `next.startsWith('-')` rejection branch; `process.exit(2)`; core's `loadConfig(path)` which already throws on a missing file.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: `parley-slack --help` and `--version` now print to stdout and exit 0 before any transport exists (the redis CLI comment explicitly sanctions stdout on a branch that exits before the transport).
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `parley-slack --config` (no value), `parley-slack --config -x`, `parley-slack --config=`, `parley-slack extra.yaml`, `parley-slack --verbose` — all of which today start a bridge on the default config, and after the fix exit 2 with usage on stderr.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I grepped `packages/bridge-slack/test/*.ts` for `cli` and found no importer, and core's packaging.test.ts only checks that the `bin` target is emitted and resolvable, not its argument behaviour.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes the silent wrong-workspace start outright. If left unfixed, nothing else compensates: the only signal today is the ABSENCE of a stderr line, and an MCP stdio host routinely discards a child's stderr.

summary: The WAKE ELIGIBILITY table (declared CLASS (2): "A parked long-poll must wake only on an event STRICTLY above its own floor") cannot fail on the guard it exists to grade. Its oracle rests on a stated premise that is false about the code: "a waiter woken below its floor re-queries, finds nothing, and returns an empty page at once — turning `block_ms` back into the busy-return loop it exists to remove." `blockForMessage` does not return on an empty re-query; it advances `floor`, re-arms a waiter and loops. So a spurious wake costs one extra `conversations.history` read and one extra iteration, and the call still holds its full budget — which is exactly what the rows assert (`elapsed >= BLOCK_MS * 0.8`, `messages === []`).
failure: Mutation applied and verified at packages/bridge-slack/src/link.ts:374: replace `if (compareTs(event.ts, waiter.since) > 0) waiter.wake();` with an unconditional `waiter.wake();`. blocking-fetch.test.ts (53 tests) and envelope-robustness.test.ts (25 tests) both stay green — 78/78 passed. Every one of the five ELIGIBILITY rows, including 'stays parked through an event exactly at the floor' and 'stays parked through an event below the floor', and 'two waiters at different floors on one channel: only the eligible one wakes', passes with the floor comparison deleted. A `>=`-for-`>` slip would be equally invisible.
remediation: Grade the observable the guard actually protects — request cost, not elapsed time. In each non-waking ELIGIBILITY row, snapshot `fake.hits('conversations.history')` immediately before the event is landed and assert it is unchanged when the call returns (a spurious wake costs exactly one extra read plus a re-arm); in the waking row assert the read happened. Correct the docstring's stated failure mode to "a spurious wake costs one tiered `conversations.history` read per below-floor event on the channel", which is what the guard buys.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the eligibility rows over the floor-relative offset rather than over three hand-written cases: `[-60s, -1 suffix tick, exactly the floor, +1 suffix tick, +60s]`, crossed with `{same channel, other channel}` and with `{one waiter, two waiters at different floors}`, and assert per row (a) the resulting `conversations.history` read delta and (b) whether the page carries the event. The `+1 suffix tick` row is the one that separates `>` from `>=`; the read-delta assertion is the one that separates 'floor honoured' from 'floor ignored'. The same widening applies to any future per-waiter predicate — key the row on the predicate's input, and the assertion on the work the predicate saves.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `FakeSlack.hits(method)` (incremented before the auth check, so it means 'reached the wire'), `FakeSlack.pushEvent` for landing an event at an arbitrary `ts`, and the harness's `parkedWaiters` probe.

summary: blocking-fetch.test.ts costs ~105 s for 53 rows, and almost none of them can fail on the native-wake path the file's headline CLASS (1) is about. The lost-wakeup table's bound is `elapsed < blockMs / 2`, but the degradation ladder re-reads history at 500 ms unconditionally — so at `blockMs = 3000` the ladder alone returns the message at ~500 ms, well under 1500 ms, whatever the socket did. Half the table (every `blockMs = 3000` row) is therefore graded by the ladder, not by the wake.
failure: Mutation applied and verified at packages/bridge-slack/src/link.ts:370-375: remove the entire waiter-wake block from `routeEnvelope`, so a live push NEVER wakes a parked long-poll. 51 of 53 rows still pass; only 'wakes natively when the message lands during the gap-closing re-query (blockMs=800)' and '… after the waiter is parked (blockMs=800)' fail. The whole `blockMs = 3000` half of the STAGES table, and 'a handshake that recovers mid-budget still wakes natively', pass with the native wake entirely gone.

Keep one long-budget row explicitly labelled as the ladder control.
testUpgrade: Make the table's discriminating power explicit rather than incidental: parameterize the wake rows over `blockMs` and assert `elapsed < rungStarts(blockMs)[1]` (the first ladder rung) — a bound only a native wake can meet, at every budget. That guards the CLASS 'a latency assertion that a fallback path can satisfy', which will recur for any backend whose blocking fetch has both a push and a poll path; the current `blockMs / 2` shape passes for every budget above 2 × DIAL_BACKOFF_MS.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `DIAL_BACKOFF_MS` and the `rungStarts(blockMs)` helper already exported from harness.ts and derived from the plugin's own constants.

'a handshake that recovers mid-budget still wakes natively' (blockMs 5000, bound 2500 ms) would need the same treatment or an explicit relabel as a ladder control; I did not run the amended file.

summary: In `blockForMessage`, the waiter is armed before the gap-closing re-query (correct) and woken on the success path, but a REJECTING `runFetch` propagates out of the loop with the waiter still registered. It self-clears at its own rung timer (≤ MAX_DIAL_BACKOFF_MS = 5 s), so this is a bounded leak, not a permanent one — but until then it holds a live timer and is iterated by every live event on that channel, against a caller that is already gone. `armWaiter`'s docstring claims the handle fires "EXACTLY once, self-cleaning", and `withBlocking` in blocking-fetch.test.ts claims to cover every exit ("woken, timed out, aborted by `disconnect()`, or released by a socket loss") — the rejection exit is a fifth exit neither statement accounts for.
failure: `fake.onHit('conversations.history', hit => { if (hit === 1) fake.failMethod('conversations.history','internal_error'); })`, then `plugin.fetchRecent({ topic, since: asCursor('0'), blockMs: 3000 })` → the call rejects with `SlackApiError: Slack conversations.history → internal_error` and `parkedWaiters(plugin)` is 1 immediately afterwards (reproduced in this worktree; the helper's own assertion `expect(parkedWaiters(plugin)).toBe(0)` fails).
remediation: Wrap the re-query so the waiter is released on every exit: `let requeried; try { requeried = await this.runFetch({ ...args, since: floor }); } catch (e) { wake(); throw e; }` — or hoist `wake()` into a `finally` and drop the explicit success-path call, since `armWaiter`'s `wake` is already idempotent (`wake: () => { if (done) return; done = true; clearTimeout(timer); … }`).

summary: README says `observed_max_chats` bounds "at most `observed_max_chats` *unserved* chats **plus** the chats this bridge serves" and gives the sizing formula `observed_retention_per_chat × (observed_max_chats + the number of topics you point at this bridge)`. `admit()` tests `this.byChat.size < this.maxChats`, and `byChat` includes the SERVED chats — so the unserved budget is `maxChats − (served chats holding records)`, not `maxChats`. `applyChatCap()` has the same accounting on load.

Zero, where the README row promises up to three. Every inbound message from an unconfigured chat is silently refused (one throttled stderr line per minute). An operator with 5 `chat_map` topics who sets `observed_max_chats: 5` to keep a handful of drive-by chats keeps none.

Enforcing the doc means counting only unserved chats: `admit` -> `if (this.unservedCount() < this.maxChats) return true;` and `applyChatCap` -> `while (this.unservedCount() > this.maxChats && this.evictLeastRecentUnserved())`, with `unservedCount()` counting `byChat` keys absent from `served`. Keeping the code means rewriting the README row and the sizing formula to say the cap bounds the store's TOTAL chats, of which the served ones are never the eviction victims — and updating `docs.test.ts`'s `forbids:/max distinct chats kept in the store/i` accordingly.

Replace the `<=` with an EXECUTED cell that derives its expectation from the documented formula: a table over `(servedChats, floodChats, cap)` including rows where `served >= cap` — exactly where the two arithmetics diverge and where every existing row avoids going — asserting `keptUnserved === min(flood, cap)` for the documented semantics plus all served chats retained. `store.test.ts` currently hard-codes the OPPOSITE, `Math.max(0, Math.min(flood, maxChats - served))`, locking the implementation in against its own README; that expression is the one to re-derive from the doc.

That is more attacker-influenced state retained — bounded by `retention × maxChats` on top of the served chats, which is exactly what the README already tells the operator to size for.

summary: `StoreLock.replaceStale` publishes a take-over under a `<store_path>.lock.break` sibling created with `flag:'wx'` and unlinked in a `finally`. A `finally` does not run when the process dies (SIGKILL, OOM, power loss) between the create and the rename — and nothing ever ages out or liveness-checks the break sibling. Once one is orphaned, EVERY future stale-claim take-over fails at the first `writeFileSync(...,'wx')` (EEXIST -> `return false`), so the README's "A claim naming a process that is gone is a crashed bridge's leftover and is replaced automatically" is permanently false for that store path.
failure: Reproduced in-worktree: with `store.jsonl.lock` naming a dead pid (999999) and an orphaned `store.jsonl.lock.break` present, `new StoreFile(store.jsonl)` throws `ObservedStore: '…/store.jsonl' is already claimed by process 999999 through '…/store.jsonl.lock'. … If no such process is running, remove '…/store.jsonl.lock'.` The bridge will not start; the operator follows the message, removes `.lock`, and starts — but `.lock.break` is still there, so the NEXT crash wedges the bridge again, indefinitely.
remediation: Apply the same liveness rule to the break sibling that `claim()` already applies to the claim: on EEXIST, read its pid via `lockHolder(this.breakPath)` and, when it names no live process (or carries nothing readable), unlink it and retry the exclusive create ONCE before giving up. Alternatively name the break sibling per-pid (`<path>.lock.break.<pid>`) so an orphan can never collide with a live take-over, and sweep dead-pid siblings on claim. Either way, name `<path>.lock.break` in the claim-failure message so a wedged operator can see it.
testUpgrade: `store-lock-race.test.ts` sweeps the interleaving axis thoroughly but never grades LEFTOVER on-disk state. Add a second axis — the sibling debris a crashed bridge can leave — as a table over `{no debris, orphan .lock.break with a dead pid, orphan .lock.break with a live pid, orphan .lock.break with garbage content}` crossed with `{stale .lock, no .lock, live .lock}`, asserting the invariant the existing sweep asserts: exactly one holder, and the store is claimable whenever no live process holds it. Also assert at the end of every existing interleaving row that no `.lock.break` survives a completed claim — that check alone catches the class from the other direction.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `StoreLock.replaceStale`'s `writeFileSync(this.breakPath, …, {flag:'wx'})` whose `catch { return false; }` swallows EEXIST, plus the existing `lockHolder()` and `processExists()` helpers (`processExists` treats EPERM as alive, so a break sibling naming another user's live pid is correctly left alone).
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A start that today fails: a stale `.lock` plus a `.lock.break` whose pid is dead. The claim then proceeds, which is the intended crash recovery.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I read store-lock-race.test.ts in full; its 12 interleaving rows never pre-create a `.lock.break`, and its `afterEach` rmrf's the whole tmpdir, so no row observes break-sibling debris. store-single-writer.test.ts asserts the second-bridge refusal against a LIVE holder, which this fix does not touch (`processExists` returns true there).
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If the break sibling is merely swept unconditionally (rather than pid-checked) while the underlying race remains, two starters that both saw the same dead pid can each clear the other's in-progress take-over and both end up holding the store — the exact two-writers state store-lock-race.test.ts was written to prevent, and a strictly worse outcome than the wedge.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Two starters racing on a stale `.lock` with an orphan `.lock.break`: A and B both hit EEXIST, both read the dead pid off the break sibling, both unlink it, both retry `wx`. Exactly one wins the retry (O_EXCL); the loser returns false and reports the claim as held, which is the existing safe outcome. The dangerous ordering is A unlinking a break sibling B had just legitimately created — so the unlink must be conditional on the pid A actually READ being dead, and the retry must be a single non-looping attempt, or A can livelock B out. I have NOT executed this interleaving; the existing harness's syscall-boundary sweep is the right instrument for it.

So `backend_config.service: 'xmpp://127.999.999.999:5222'` suppresses the ONLY warning on a path where @xmpp/client registers SASL PLAIN unconditionally and an on-path attacker who strips <starttls/> is handed the password — while every other backend warns on the same host. `127.00.0.1` behaves identically. summary: The cursor was hardened to carry store identity (`<storeId>.<rowid>`) precisely so a read position minted by a previous store generation cannot silently skip history. The dedup key was not: `post()` returns `String(info.lastInsertRowid)` and `rowToMessage` sets `id: String(row.id)`, a bare rowid that restarts at 1 on every fresh store. Core's `SeenSet` (packages/bridge-core/src/engine/seen-set.ts) keys on topic + backendMsgId with no generation component, so a second generation's ids 1..N are indistinguishable from the first's. The README documents the hazard and prescribes "restart the bridge", i.e. the plugin knowingly leaves the paired key unprotected against the exact scenario the cursor prefix exists for.
failure: Trace (not reproduced end to end): an embedder — or any future core reconnect path — does `connect(A)` → `catchUpTopic(T)` (SeenSet records ids '1'..'N' under T) → `disconnect()` → `connect(B)` onto a reset or replaced store → `catchUpTopic(T)`. Plugin-side everything is correct: the stale cursor is foreign, `resumeAfter` returns 0n and the topic replays in full. Core then drops every replayed message whose new rowid collides with a recorded one — the messages are lost from the agent's view with no error and no log, which is the failure mode the cursor prefix was introduced to end. test/catchup-live-handoff.test.ts's `a reconnect onto a different store does not inherit the old one's hand-off point` drives exactly this sequence with a shared `SeenSet`, but only asserts the live path, so the dedup collision is never observed. Not reachable through the shipped `parley-sqlite` CLI, which connects once.
remediation: Either (a) mint `backendMsgId` with the same prefix the cursor carries (`<storeId>.<rowid>`), keeping `post()`'s return and `rowToMessage`'s `id` deriving from one helper as `mintCursor` already does — note this changes the value stored in `in_reply_to`, so a migration or a parse-both reader is needed; or (b) if the asymmetry is deliberate, surface it at the seam rather than in prose — e.g. have core scope its seen-set by the plugin-supplied generation — which is a core change and therefore, per the prime directive, a finding about the seam rather than something this plugin should absorb.

Add a shared case to the conformance suite (it already owns the cursor-vs-dedup-key contract via `post-id-agreement`): drive `connect → catchUp → disconnect → reset-or-replace-store → connect → catchUp` against one `SeenSet`, and assert every message of the second generation is surfaced. Parameterized over the fixture's existing reset hook, it grades every backend whose ids are store-local (sqlite rowids, telegram's local sequence), not just this instance.

remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Under (a), any consumer that assumes `backendMsgId` is numeric — including this package's own `in_reply_to` column, which today stores the bare rowid and would begin storing a prefixed string, and src/index.test.ts's `backendMsgId is the bare rowid` case which asserts the current spelling.

summary: The plugin is one class spread across a five-deep inheritance chain — PluginState -> PostgresPush -> PostgresListener -> PostgresListen -> PostgresPlugin — where every intermediate is `abstract` with exactly one subclass and no variant. Inheritance here buys nothing polymorphism-shaped; it is a namespace for splitting one file, and its cost is that all 14 pieces of mutable state in PluginState are `protected` and reachable from every layer, so the layer boundaries constrain nothing.
failure: Not a runtime failure — a design cost. Concretely: `state.ts` declares `subs`, `waiters`, `listens`, `pendingAborts`, `starting`, `epoch`, `stopped`, `listener`, `listenerPromise`, `reconnecting` as shared protected fields, and the teardown correctness argument in index.ts:164-193 depends on knowing which of five files may touch each of them at which moment. There is also a declaration cycle held open only by `import type` erasure: state.ts imports `TopicSubscription` from push.ts and `ListenState` from listen.ts, while push.ts imports `PluginState` from state.ts. Converting one of those to a value import at any point makes it a runtime cycle.
remediation: Replace the chain with composition: a `ListenerConnection` object owning the socket, the memo, the reconnect loop and the LISTEN refcounts; a `Subscriptions` object owning the drain loop and its backoff; and `PostgresPlugin` holding both. Each then has a narrow constructor-injected surface instead of shared protected fields, and the teardown ordering becomes an explicit sequence of calls rather than an invariant spread across five files. I hold this loosely — the same shape appears across the decomposed backends, so it may be a repo-scoped decision rather than this package's.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a structural assertion or a structure that cements a shape'. Per CLAUDE.md's standing rule, do NOT add a test asserting the class layout. Instead, grade the invariant the chain currently protects from a place a refactor cannot invalidate: assert through the PUBLIC seam that after `disconnect()` no registry retains an entry and no socket survives — connection-hygiene.test.ts already does this via `registrySizes(priv)`, but it reaches private fields by cast, which is exactly the shape-lock the rule warns about. Rewrite that post-condition as `settledBackendCount(appName) === 0` plus a behavioural probe (a post to a previously-subscribed topic delivers nothing), so it survives the composition refactor.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: Nothing yet — I did not attempt the refactor. It would touch every `this.` reference across push.ts, listener.ts, listen.ts and index.ts.

remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: connection-hygiene.test.ts and teardown-races-setup.test.ts both cast the plugin to a `Priv` interface naming `subs`, `subscribing`, `listens`, `waiters`, `pendingAborts`, `starting`, `pool`, `listener`, `listenerPromise` as instance fields; moving any of them into a composed object breaks those casts at compile time. retention.test.ts's `priv.pruneTimer` and prune-bounded.test.ts's `(plugin as any).prune` binding are the same.
